core.p: Free fall is just constant acceleration with a = 10 m/s², so you use the equations from 2.8 and 2.9. Choose downwards as positive to avoid sign confusion.
bullets: Change in velocity: v = u + a t, or a = (v - u) / t with a = 10 m/s².
Speed after falling a height x from rest: v² - u² = 2 a x, so v² = 2 x 10 x x.
Height fallen in time t from rest: area under the velocity-time graph = 1/2 x t x (10t).

A ball **thrown upwards** decelerates at 10 m/s² on the way up, stops momentarily at the top, then accelerates down at 10 m/s². Its acceleration is 10 m/s² downwards **the whole time**, even at the top.
Answers are **ideal values** because air resistance is ignored; real objects reach lower speeds.

callouts.t: At the top of a throw
callouts.p: Velocity is zero at the highest point, but acceleration is still 10 m/s² downwards. Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration.

core.p: You also need to estimate the size of accelerations in everyday life. Use a typical change in speed and a sensible time, then a = change in velocity / time. Comparing the answer with g (10 m/s²) helps you judge whether it is realistic.
bullets: Car pulling away: 0 to 13 m/s in about 5 s gives about **2 to 3 m/s²**.
Sprinter at the start: 0 to 10 m/s in about 2 s gives about **5 m/s²**.
Bus or train pulling away: roughly **0.5 to 1.5 m/s²**, gentle so standing passengers do not fall.
Car braking hard (emergency stop): a deceleration of roughly **7 m/s²**, a little under g.
Car crash: stopping from 13 m/s in about 0.1 s gives a deceleration of over **100 m/s²**, more than 10 g, which is why crashes are so dangerous (see 2.31).
Accelerations are often compared with g: '3 g' means 30 m/s².

callouts.p: If you estimate a car accelerating at 50 m/s² or a person walking at 15 m/s, something has gone wrong: check your units and assumptions.

core.p: Combining the methods above lets you measure the acceleration due to gravity. This is a good example of applying the speed-measuring techniques to free fall.
bullets: Drop an object with a card (or a picket fence card) through **two light gates** one above the other, or through one gate with a double interrupt card.
Find the speed at each gate and the time between them, then a = (v - u) / t.
Or measure the speed at a gate a measured height x below the release point and use v² = 2 g x.
Use a **dense, compact** object so air resistance is small compared with weight.
Results are usually close to 9.8 m/s²; values a little low are caused by air resistance and friction.

callouts.p: Air resistance is then much smaller than the weight, so the motion is close to true free fall.

analogy.t: The light gate as a turnstile counter
analogy.p: A light gate works like a turnstile that times how long each person takes to push through. If you know how wide each person is (the card length) and how long they block the turnstile (the time), you know how fast they were walking. Free fall is like a bank account that adds exactly 10 m/s of speed into your 'velocity account' every second. Where it breaks down: a turnstile physically slows people down, but a light beam exerts no force and does not change the trolley's speed, and real falling objects have air resistance that 'taxes' the deposits so the gain becomes less than 10 m/s each second as speed rises.

terms.d: The distance travelled per unit time; a scalar measured in m/s.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken.
The speed at a particular instant, found by measuring over a very short distance or time.
A sensor that detects an object breaking a light beam and, with a timer or data logger, measures how long the beam is blocked.
An electronic device that automatically records readings from sensors over time and can calculate speed and acceleration.
The time between a person seeing an event and responding to it; typically about 0.2 to 0.3 s.
A device that marks dots on paper tape 50 times per second, so each gap represents 0.02 s.
A card with two solid sections and a gap, which breaks a light gate beam twice so one gate can give two speeds and an acceleration.
An error that makes readings scatter unpredictably around the true value; reduced by repeating and taking a mean.
An error that shifts all readings by the same amount or in the same direction, such as a zero error or always reacting late.
The rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t, measured in m/s².
Motion when the only force acting on an object is its weight, so it accelerates at g.
The acceleration of a freely falling object near the Earth's surface, about 10 m/s².
A frictional force opposing motion through air, which increases as speed increases.
The constant maximum velocity reached when air resistance equals weight, so the resultant force and acceleration are zero.
An approximate value found using sensible typical values and simple calculation, usually to 1 or 2 significant figures.

mistakes.w: Using light gates makes the experiment more fair.
mistakes.r: Light gates remove human reaction time, so the time is measured more accurately (they do not affect fairness).

mistakes.w: Speed = time blocked / length of card.
mistakes.r: Speed = length of card / time beam is blocked (distance divided by time).

mistakes.w: Walking speed is about 5 m/s.
mistakes.r: Walking is about 1.5 m/s; running about 3 m/s; cycling about 6 m/s.

mistakes.w: Heavier objects fall faster in free fall.
mistakes.r: All objects in free fall have the same acceleration, g = 10 m/s², whatever their mass.

mistakes.w: g is 10 m/s, or the object falls at 10 m/s.
mistakes.r: g is an acceleration of 10 m/s²: the velocity increases by 10 m/s every second.

mistakes.w: At the top of its flight a thrown ball has zero acceleration.
mistakes.r: Its velocity is zero at the top but its acceleration is still 10 m/s² downwards.

mistakes.w: Repeat the readings to make them accurate.
mistakes.r: Repeat readings and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of random errors (improves the reliability of the mean).

mistakes.w: Using a card length of 5 cm directly: 5 / 0.1 = 50 m/s.
mistakes.r: Convert to metres first: 0.05 m / 0.1 s = 0.5 m/s.

mistakes.w: Speed of sound is about 3 x 10^8 m/s.
mistakes.r: That is the speed of light. Sound in air travels at about 330 to 340 m/s.

exam.q: State the acceleration of an object in free fall near the Earth's surface.
model: 10 m/s² (accept 9.8 or 9.81 m/s²)
exam.tip: Include the unit m/s²; m/s is wrong.

exam.q: Which of these is a typical speed for a person cycling? A 0.6 m/s B 6 m/s C 60 m/s D 600 m/s
model: B (6 m/s)
exam.tip: Learn walk 1.5, run 3, cycle 6 m/s.

exam.q: Give a typical value for the speed of sound in air.
model: Any value from 330 to 340 m/s
exam.tip: Do not confuse with the speed of light.

exam.q: A student times a trolley over 0.50 m with a stopwatch. Explain why using a light gate would give a more accurate value of speed.
model: Light gate removes human reaction time / no human error in starting and stopping the timer
The time is short so reaction time is a large fraction of it / light gate measures time to a higher resolution
exam.tip: Always link the improvement to reaction time.

exam.q: A card of length 4.0 cm on a trolley blocks a light gate for 0.050 s. Calculate the speed of the trolley.
exam.tip: Convert cm to m before dividing.

exam.q: A stone is dropped from rest from a bridge and hits the water 2.0 s later. Assuming air resistance is negligible, calculate its speed as it hits the water.
model: v = 20 m/s
exam.tip: Free fall means a = 10 m/s²; use a = (v - u) / t rearranged.

exam.q: Estimate the acceleration of a car that speeds up from rest to a typical town speed. State any values you assume.
model: Sensible final speed assumed, e.g. 13 m/s
Sensible time assumed, e.g. 5 s (accept 3 to 10 s)
a = 13 / 5 = about 2.6 m/s² (answer consistent with assumptions, roughly 1 to 5 m/s²)
exam.tip: Write down your assumed values; marks are given for sensible ones.

exam.q: Estimate how far a student walks in 15 minutes.
model: Assume walking speed about 1.5 m/s
15 min = 900 s
distance = 1.5 x 900 = 1350 m, about 1.4 km (accept 1 to 2 km)
exam.tip: Convert minutes to seconds.

exam.q: Explain why a feather falls more slowly than a hammer on Earth, but at the same rate on the Moon.
model: On Earth air resistance acts on both objects
Air resistance is large compared with the feather's weight so its acceleration is much less than g
The Moon has no atmosphere so only weight acts and both are in free fall with the same acceleration
exam.tip: Free fall means weight is the only force acting.

exam.q: Describe how you could use light gates to measure the acceleration of a trolley rolling down a ramp.
model: Fix a card of measured length to the trolley and place two light gates on the ramp connected to a data logger
Speed at each gate = card length / time beam is blocked, giving u and v
Record the time taken to travel between the gates (or measure the distance between gates)
a = (v - u) / t (or a = (v² - u²) / 2x)
exam.tip: Say what is measured, with what, and which equation is used.

exam.q: Describe and evaluate methods a student could use to measure the speed of a remote-controlled toy car moving across a laboratory floor.
model: Method 1: mark a measured distance (e.g. 2 m) with a tape measure and time the car with a stopwatch
speed = distance / time
Stopwatch timing affected by human reaction time (about 0.2 to 0.3 s), which is significant for short times
Improve by using a longer distance and repeating to calculate a mean
Method 2: light gates connected to a data logger with a card of known length on the car, speed = card length / time blocked (or two gates a known distance apart)

Light gates remove reaction time and measure time more precisely, so give a more accurate speed (closer to instantaneous speed); video analysis with a scale and known frame rate is another valid method
exam.tip: 6 mark answers need a method, the equation, and a judgement comparing accuracy, with reasons.

worked.q: A trolley carrying a 10 cm card passes through gate A in 0.125 s and gate B in 0.050 s. It takes 0.60 s to travel between the gates. Calculate its acceleration.
A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 5.0 m. Ignoring air resistance, calculate the speed with which it hits the ground.
During a thunderstorm a student counts 4 s between seeing the lightning and hearing the thunder. Estimate how far away the storm is.
steps: Light travels so fast that it arrives almost instantly, so the 4 s delay is the time for the sound.
Assume speed of sound in air = 340 m/s.

phy_edx.1.5.summary: Newton's first law says that an object **remains at rest or continues to move at a constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it**. When the forces on an object are **balanced** (resultant force zero) it either stays still or keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction. When the forces are **unbalanced** (resultant force not zero) the object's **speed and/or direction** changes, which means it accelerates. You must be able to find a resultant force, draw free-body diagrams and use the law to explain everyday situations such as cars, falling objects and spacecraft.

core.p: A force is a push or a pull. It has both **size (magnitude)** and **direction**, so it is a **vector** quantity (2.1 to 2.5). This matters because forces acting in opposite directions can cancel, and to know what an object will do you must combine all the forces into one **resultant force**.
bullets: Forces are measured in **newtons (N)**.
On diagrams, forces are drawn as **arrows**: the length shows the size and the arrowhead shows the direction.

Common forces: **weight** (gravity, acts downwards), **normal contact force** (reaction, acts at right angles to a surface), **friction** and **air resistance/drag** (oppose motion), **driving force/thrust** (pushes forward), **tension** (in a rope or string) and **upthrust** (in fluids).
Each force acts **on** a particular object; when using Newton's first law only consider forces acting on the object you are studying.

callouts.p: A quantity with magnitude and direction. Force, velocity, acceleration, displacement and momentum are vectors.

core.p: The **resultant force** is the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined. For forces along a straight line you simply add those in one direction and subtract those in the opposite direction.
bullets: Forces in the **same direction**: add them. 20 N right + 30 N right = 50 N right.
Forces in **opposite directions**: subtract the smaller from the larger. The resultant acts in the direction of the larger force.
Example: 50 N right and 30 N left gives a resultant of **20 N to the right**.
Always give the **direction** as well as the size of a resultant force.
Pick one direction as positive (for example right or forwards) and treat the opposite direction as negative to avoid sign errors.
If the forces add to zero, the resultant force is **0 N**.

callouts.p: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object; the vector sum of all the forces.

fig.cap: Forces of 50 N to the right and 30 N to the left act on a box. They are unbalanced, so the resultant force is 50 - 30 = 20 N to the right and the box accelerates to the right.

core.p: Whether the forces on an object are balanced or unbalanced decides whether its motion changes. This is the heart of Newton's first law.
bullets: **Balanced forces**: the forces cancel out, so the **resultant force is zero**.
**Unbalanced forces**: the forces do not cancel, so there is a **non-zero resultant force**.
Balanced forces do **not** mean there are no forces; it means the forces add up to zero.
Balanced forces do **not** mean the object is stationary; it could be moving at a constant velocity.
Unbalanced forces always cause a **change in velocity** (an **acceleration**), which could be speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

head: Balanced forces
Unbalanced forces
rows: Starts to move in direction of resultant
Not zero, in direction of resultant force

callouts.t: Moving does not need a force
callouts.p: A force is needed to change motion, not to keep an object moving. A car at a steady 30 m/s on a straight road has balanced forces.

core.p: Newton's first law describes what happens when the resultant force on an object is zero or not zero. It tells us that objects naturally keep doing what they are already doing; only a resultant force changes that.
bullets: If the resultant force on a **stationary** object is zero, it **remains stationary**.
If the resultant force on a **moving** object is zero, it **continues to move at the same speed in the same direction** (constant velocity).
If the resultant force is **not zero**, the object's **velocity changes**: its speed changes, its direction changes, or both.
The change in velocity is in the **direction of the resultant force** (how big the change is comes from F = m a in 2.15).
Constant velocity means **both** constant speed **and** constant direction (a straight line).

callouts.p: An object will remain at rest, or continue to move at a constant velocity, unless it is acted on by a resultant force.
Mark schemes want 'resultant force is zero' or 'forces are balanced'. Writing 'there is no force' is wrong when forces are acting.

core.h: Situation A: resultant force zero and object at rest
core.p: An object resting on a surface has forces acting on it, but they are balanced, so it stays at rest.
bullets: A book on a table: its **weight** acts downwards and the **normal contact force** from the table acts upwards.
The two forces are **equal in size and opposite in direction**, so the resultant force is zero.
Therefore the book **remains at rest**.
A hanging lamp: its weight down is balanced by the **tension** in the cable up.
A boat floating still: weight down is balanced by **upthrust** up.
If a sideways push is applied but the object does not move, then **friction** is equal and opposite to the push (until the push is big enough to overcome the maximum friction).

callouts.p: Weight and normal contact force on a book are balanced forces on the SAME object (first law). A third-law pair acts on DIFFERENT objects and is always of the same type of force.

fig.cap: A book at rest on a table and its free-body diagram. The weight and the normal contact force are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero and the book stays at rest.

core.h: Situation A: resultant force zero and object moving at constant velocity
core.p: This is the part of the law that surprises people: an object can be moving with **no resultant force** at all. If the forces are balanced it simply keeps going at the same speed in the same direction.
bullets: A car travelling at a **steady speed on a straight road**: the **driving force** forwards equals the **resistive forces** (air resistance plus friction) backwards, so the resultant is zero and velocity is constant.
A skydiver at **terminal velocity**: weight downwards equals air resistance upwards.
A space probe far from any planet or star: there is almost no force on it at all, so it keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed **without needing its engines**.
A puck sliding on smooth ice: friction is very small, so it keeps going almost at constant velocity.
The engine of a car at constant velocity is still working hard, but only to **balance** the resistive forces, not to make the car go faster.

callouts.p: Constant velocity (including zero velocity) always means resultant force = 0. Read 'steady speed in a straight line' as 'forces balanced'.

fig.cap: A car moving at constant velocity. The driving force equals the resistive forces and the weight equals the normal contact force, so the resultant force is zero.

core.h: Situation B: resultant force not zero changes the speed
core.p: When the forces along the direction of motion are unbalanced, the object speeds up or slows down. The direction of the resultant force compared with the direction of motion tells you which.
bullets: Resultant force **in the same direction** as motion: the object **speeds up** (accelerates).
Resultant force **opposite** to the direction of motion: the object **slows down** (decelerates).
A car pulling away: driving force is **greater than** resistive forces, so there is a resultant force forwards and the car speeds up.
A car braking: braking force plus resistive forces act backwards with no driving force, so the resultant is backwards and the car slows down.
A stationary object pushed by a resultant force **starts moving** in the direction of that force.
As a car speeds up, air resistance increases until it equals the driving force; the forces are then balanced and the car moves at a constant (top) speed.

callouts.p: In explanations always compare: 'the driving force is greater than the resistive force, so there is a resultant force forwards, so the car accelerates'.

core.h: Situation B: resultant force not zero changes the direction
core.p: A resultant force does not have to change speed. If it acts at an angle to the motion it changes the **direction** of motion. Because velocity includes direction, a change of direction is still a change of velocity, so the object is accelerating.
bullets: A resultant force at **right angles** to the motion changes the direction but not the speed.

An object moving in a **circle at constant speed** has a constantly changing direction, so its velocity is changing and there must be a resultant force acting towards the centre (developed further in 2.20 to 2.21).
Examples: the Moon orbiting the Earth (gravity), a ball whirled on a string (tension), a car going round a bend (friction between tyres and road).
If the resultant force suddenly disappears (the string breaks), the object carries on in a **straight line** at constant speed, exactly as the first law predicts.
A thrown ball follows a curved path because its weight acts at an angle to its velocity, changing both its speed and direction.

callouts.p: Constant speed in a circle is not constant velocity. There is a resultant force, so the forces are unbalanced.

core.p: A **free-body diagram** shows the object on its own (often as a box or dot) with an arrow for every force acting **on** it. It is the best way to decide whether forces are balanced.
bullets: Draw the object as a simple shape or a dot.
Draw each force as an arrow starting **from the object**, pointing in the direction the force acts.
Make the arrow **length proportional to the size** of the force; equal forces have equal-length arrows.
**Label** each arrow with the name of the force (and its size if known).
Do **not** include forces that the object exerts on other things.
Then find the resultant in each direction (vertical and horizontal) separately.
If both the vertical and horizontal resultants are zero, the object is at rest or at constant velocity.

callouts.p: If a question says an object is accelerating, your arrows must NOT be equal in that direction. Examiners check this.

core.h: Applying the first law to a falling object
core.p: A skydiver is a classic six-mark context because the resultant force changes throughout the fall. Newton's first law explains the stages of constant velocity; unbalanced forces explain the stages of changing speed.
bullets: Just after jumping: speed is low so **air resistance is small**; weight is much bigger, so there is a **large resultant force downwards** and the skydiver accelerates.
As speed increases, **air resistance increases**, so the resultant force decreases and the acceleration decreases.
When **air resistance equals weight**, the forces are **balanced**, the resultant is zero and the skydiver falls at a constant velocity called **terminal velocity**.
Opening the parachute increases the surface area, so air resistance becomes **greater than weight**; the resultant force is **upwards**, so the skydiver **slows down** (still moving downwards).
As speed falls, air resistance decreases until it equals weight again, giving a new, **lower terminal velocity**.
The same reasoning explains a car reaching top speed: driving force constant, air resistance rising with speed until balanced.

head: Stage
Forces
Resultant
Motion
rows: Weight much bigger than air resistance

callouts.t: Parachute does not make you go up
callouts.p: An upward resultant force while moving down makes the skydiver slow down; it does not reverse the direction of motion.

core.h: Why the first law seems to go against everyday experience
core.p: On Earth, things we push usually stop when we stop pushing, so it seems as though a force is needed to keep things moving. In fact they stop because of **friction and air resistance**, which are forces. Remove those forces and the object keeps moving forever.
bullets: A ball rolling across grass slows and stops because **friction** provides a resultant force opposite to its motion.
The same ball on smooth ice travels much further because friction is smaller.
Spacecraft such as Voyager keep travelling through space for decades with engines off because there is almost no resistive force.
The reason we have to keep pressing a car's accelerator at steady speed is to **balance** the resistive forces, not to 'supply motion'.
This tendency of an object to keep doing what it is doing is linked to its **mass**; the idea of inertial mass is developed in 2.22.

callouts.p: Objects slow down because a resultant force (usually friction or drag) acts against their motion, not because they 'run out' of force.

core.p: Most marks on this point come from clear chains of reasoning. Link the forces to the resultant, and the resultant to the motion, in that order.
bullets: Step 1: name the forces acting and their directions.
Step 2: **compare** their sizes (equal, greater, smaller).
Step 3: state the **resultant force** (zero, or its direction).
Step 4: state the effect on the **motion** (at rest / constant velocity / speeds up / slows down / changes direction).
Use precise words: 'constant velocity', 'resultant force', 'balanced', 'unbalanced', 'accelerates', 'decelerates'.
For calculations, always include the **unit (N)** and the **direction** of the resultant.

callouts.p: Forces compared, then resultant, then motion. For example: 'air resistance equals weight, so resultant force is zero, so the skydiver moves at constant velocity'.

analogy.p: Newton's first law is like a tug of war with a rope on a smooth floor. If both teams pull equally hard (balanced forces) the knot in the middle stays where it is, or if it was already sliding it keeps sliding at the same rate. Only when one team pulls harder (unbalanced forces) does the knot's motion change, towards the stronger team (the direction of the resultant force). Where it breaks down: in a real tug of war the knot stops when both teams pull equally because of friction and the teams' feet, but in physics an object with balanced forces that is already moving keeps moving forever; also the rope can only pull along one line, whereas real forces can act at angles and change an object's direction.

terms.d: A push or pull on an object, measured in newtons (N); a vector quantity.
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
Forces whose resultant is zero, so they cause no change in the object's motion.
Forces with a non-zero resultant, which cause the object's velocity to change.
An object remains at rest or continues to move at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force.
Moving at a steady speed in a straight line (unchanging speed and direction).
The rate of change of velocity; it happens whenever speed or direction changes.
The force acting on an object due to gravity, acting downwards.
The force from a surface acting on an object at right angles to the surface.
A force that opposes motion (or attempted motion) between surfaces in contact.
A resistive force opposing the motion of an object through air, increasing as speed increases.
The forward force produced by an engine or motor that pushes a vehicle forwards.
A diagram showing an object alone with arrows for all the forces acting on it, lengths proportional to size.
The constant velocity reached by a falling object when air resistance equals its weight, so the resultant force is zero.
The pulling force exerted by a stretched string, rope or cable.

mistakes.w: The car is moving at a steady speed, so the driving force is bigger than the friction.
mistakes.r: At constant velocity the driving force equals the resistive forces; the resultant force is zero.

mistakes.w: The book is not moving, so there are no forces acting on it.
mistakes.r: Forces act (weight and normal contact force) but they are balanced, so the resultant force is zero.

mistakes.w: A force is needed to keep an object moving.
mistakes.r: A resultant force is needed to change motion; an object with no resultant force keeps moving at constant velocity.

mistakes.w: When the parachute opens the skydiver moves upwards.
mistakes.r: Air resistance becomes greater than weight, so the resultant force is upwards and the skydiver slows down (decelerates) while still falling.

mistakes.w: Resultant of 40 N left and 25 N right is 65 N.
mistakes.r: Opposite forces subtract: resultant = 15 N to the left (give size and direction).

mistakes.w: An object moving in a circle at constant speed has balanced forces.
mistakes.r: Its direction, and so its velocity, is changing, so there is a resultant force (towards the centre).

mistakes.w: Weight and normal force on a book are a Newton's third law pair.
mistakes.r: They act on the same object and are balanced forces (first law); a third-law pair acts on different objects.

mistakes.w: At terminal velocity there are no forces on the skydiver.
mistakes.r: Weight and air resistance both act and are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero.

mistakes.w: Balanced forces means the object is stationary.
mistakes.r: Balanced forces means the object is either at rest or moving at constant velocity.

exam.q: State Newton's first law of motion.
model: An object remains at rest or continues to move at constant velocity (steady speed in a straight line)
unless acted on by a resultant (unbalanced) force
exam.tip: Both parts are needed: what happens AND the condition 'unless a resultant force acts'.

exam.q: A cyclist travels at a constant velocity. What is the resultant force on the cyclist?
model: Zero (0 N)
exam.tip: Constant velocity always means zero resultant force.

exam.q: Two forces act on a box: 12 N to the left and 20 N to the right. Calculate the resultant force.
model: to the right
exam.tip: Direction is a separate mark.

exam.q: A parcel rests on the floor of a van. Draw and label the forces acting on the parcel.
model: Arrow downwards labelled weight (gravitational force)
Arrow upwards labelled normal contact force (reaction), equal in length to weight
exam.tip: Arrows of equal length show the forces are balanced.

exam.q: A boat's engine produces a forward force of 800 N. The water resistance is 800 N. Describe the motion of the boat.
model: Forces are balanced / resultant force is zero
Boat moves at constant velocity (or stays at rest if it was stationary)
exam.tip: Avoid saying 'it stops' - balanced forces do not stop a moving object.

exam.q: A space probe is travelling through deep space far from any planets. Its engines are switched off. Explain why it continues to move.
model: There is no (negligible) resultant force acting on it / no friction or air resistance in space
So by Newton's first law it continues at constant velocity
exam.tip: Mention the first law or 'constant velocity' explicitly.

exam.q: Explain why a ball whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed is accelerating.
model: Its direction of motion is continually changing
Velocity is a vector, so its velocity is changing
A changing velocity is an acceleration, which requires a resultant force (towards the centre)
exam.tip: Key idea: velocity includes direction.

exam.q: A car moves along a straight road. The driving force is 2500 N and the total resistive force is 1800 N. (a) Calculate the resultant force. (b) Describe the effect on the car's motion.
model: Resultant = 2500 - 1800 = 700 N
Forwards (in the direction of motion)
The car speeds up / accelerates
exam.tip: Link the direction of the resultant to speeding up.

exam.q: A lorry is travelling at a constant speed. The driver keeps the driving force the same but the lorry starts going up a steep hill. Explain what happens to its speed.
model: A component of the lorry's weight now acts backwards down the slope (extra force opposing motion)
Resistive forces are now greater than the driving force, so there is a resultant force backwards
The lorry slows down (decelerates)
exam.tip: Compare forces, state the resultant, then state the motion.

exam.q: A skydiver jumps from a plane and later opens a parachute. Explain, in terms of the forces acting, how the skydiver's velocity changes from leaving the plane until landing at a steady speed.
model: At first weight is greater than air resistance, so there is a resultant force downwards and the skydiver accelerates
As speed increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force (and acceleration) decreases
When air resistance equals weight the resultant force is zero and the skydiver reaches terminal velocity (constant velocity)
When the parachute opens the surface area increases, so air resistance increases and becomes greater than weight
The resultant force is upwards so the skydiver decelerates (slows down while still falling)
As speed decreases air resistance decreases until it equals weight again, giving a new lower terminal velocity at which the skydiver lands
exam.tip: Six marks: one mark per stage, each with forces compared, resultant and motion.

worked.q: Three horizontal forces act on a sledge: a pull of 60 N forwards from a rope, 15 N of friction backwards and 20 N of air resistance backwards. Find the resultant force and describe the motion.
steps: The resultant is positive, so it acts forwards.
The forces are unbalanced in the direction of motion, so the sledge speeds up.
worked.ans: 25 N forwards; the sledge accelerates (speeds up).

worked.q: A lift of weight 8000 N is moving upwards at a constant speed of 2 m/s. What is the tension in its cable? Explain your answer.
steps: The lift moves at constant velocity (steady speed in a straight line).
By Newton's first law, the resultant force must be zero.
worked.ans: 8000 N, because at constant velocity the forces are balanced (the speed of 2 m/s does not matter).

worked.q: A car travelling at a steady 25 m/s on a straight motorway has a driving force of 1200 N. The driver then increases the driving force to 1500 N. Explain what happens.
steps: At 25 m/s the speed is constant, so resistive forces = driving force = 1200 N.
Immediately after the change: resultant = 1500 - 1200 = 300 N forwards.
The car accelerates, so its speed increases.
As speed increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force decreases.
When the resistive forces reach 1500 N, the forces are balanced again.
worked.ans: The car speeds up, with decreasing acceleration, until it reaches a new, higher constant speed where resistive forces equal 1500 N.

phy_edx.1.6.summary: Newton's second law links the **resultant force** on an object to its **mass** and **acceleration**: **force = mass x acceleration (F = m x a)**, an equation you must recall and use. It tells you that a bigger resultant force gives a bigger acceleration, and that the same force gives a smaller acceleration to a bigger mass. The acceleration is always in the **direction of the resultant force**. You must rearrange the equation, convert units, find the resultant force first, and combine F = m a with the motion equations in multi-step calculations.

core.p: Newton's first law (2.14) says a resultant force changes an object's velocity. The second law says **by how much**: the acceleration produced is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass. Written as an equation, this becomes F = m x a.
bullets: **force (N) = mass (kg) x acceleration (m/s²)**
Symbols: **F = m x a** (or F = ma).
F is the **resultant force**, the overall force left after all the forces have been combined.
This is an equation you must **recall**; it is not given on the equation sheet.
The acceleration is in the **same direction as the resultant force**.
If F = 0 then a = 0, so the object is at rest or moves at constant velocity, which is Newton's first law again.

callouts.p: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass: force = mass x acceleration.
F = m x a, with F in newtons (N), m in kilograms (kg) and a in metres per second squared (m/s²).

fig.cap: Equation triangle for F = m x a. Cover the quantity you want: F = m x a, m = F / a, a = F / m.

core.h: Units and what one newton means
core.p: The newton is defined using the second law. Knowing this definition helps you remember the units and check that answers make sense.
bullets: **1 newton** is the resultant force that gives a mass of **1 kg** an acceleration of **1 m/s²**.
So 1 N = 1 kg m/s².
Mass must be in **kilograms**: 500 g = 0.5 kg; 1 tonne = 1000 kg.
Acceleration must be in **m/s²**, not m/s.
Large forces may be given in kN: 1 kN = 1000 N.
Mass is a **scalar**; force and acceleration are **vectors**, so direction matters for F and a.

head: Quantity
Symbol
Unit
Common conversions
rows: Found from (v - u) / t or v² - u² = 2ax

callouts.p: A 250 g trolley is 0.25 kg. Using 250 in F = m a gives an answer 1000 times too big.

core.p: The F in F = m a is the **resultant** force, not just the biggest force or the driving force. If several forces act, combine them first, then use the resultant to find the acceleration.
bullets: Forces in the same direction add; forces in opposite directions subtract (2.14).
Example: a 10 N pull and 4 N of friction on a 2.0 kg trolley give a resultant of 6 N, so a = 6 / 2.0 = 3.0 m/s².
If you used 10 N you would wrongly get 5 m/s².
When a question gives the acceleration and asks for a **driving force**, find the resultant first using F = m a, then add on the resistive forces.
Example: a car needs a resultant of 3000 N, and resistive forces are 600 N, so the driving force must be 3600 N.

callouts.p: Look for words like 'friction', 'air resistance' or 'drag' in the question. They tell you to work out the resultant force before using F = m a.

fig.cap: A 2.0 kg trolley is pulled with 10 N against 4 N of friction. The resultant force is 6 N forwards, so the acceleration is 6 / 2.0 = 3.0 m/s² forwards.

core.p: You need to use F = m a to find any one of the three quantities. Follow a fixed routine so you never lose the method marks.
bullets: **Find force**: F = m x a. A 1200 kg car accelerating at 2.5 m/s² needs F = 1200 x 2.5 = 3000 N.
**Find acceleration**: a = F / m. A resultant of 450 N on a 90 kg cyclist gives a = 450 / 90 = 5.0 m/s².
**Find mass**: m = F / a. A resultant of 24 N gives an acceleration of 4.0 m/s², so m = 24 / 4.0 = 6.0 kg.
Routine: write the equation, convert units, substitute, rearrange, calculate, give the unit.
Give answers to a sensible number of **significant figures** (usually the same as the data, often 2 or 3).
Marks are usually given for the substitution even if the final answer is wrong, so always show working.

callouts.p: Edexcel accepts either: substitute into F = m a first and then rearrange, or rearrange to a = F / m first. Choose whichever you are less likely to get wrong.

core.h: Acceleration is proportional to force (mass constant)
core.p: For a fixed mass, doubling the resultant force doubles the acceleration. A graph of acceleration against resultant force is a **straight line through the origin**, which shows **direct proportion**.
bullets: a = F / m, so with m fixed, a is directly proportional to F.
Double F, double a; halve F, halve a.
The **gradient** of an acceleration-force graph equals **1 / m**, so a steeper line means a smaller mass.
The graph passes through the origin because zero resultant force gives zero acceleration (first law).
If friction is not compensated, the line is shifted: it crosses the force axis at a value equal to the friction force.
This relationship is tested by the core practical (2.19) using light gates or a ticker timer.

callouts.p: Straight line through the origin. Gradient of a against F = 1 / mass.

fig.cap: For a fixed mass, acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force: a straight line through the origin whose gradient is 1 / m.

core.h: Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (force constant)
core.p: For a fixed resultant force, a bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration. Doubling the mass halves the acceleration. This is why a loaded lorry speeds up much more slowly than a car even with a more powerful engine.
bullets: a = F / m, so with F fixed, a is **inversely proportional** to m.
Double m, halve a; triple m, a becomes one third.
The graph of a against m is a **curve** that gets closer to the axis but never reaches zero; a graph of a against 1 / m is a straight line through the origin.
A fully loaded lorry has a much larger mass, so the same braking force gives a smaller deceleration and a longer braking distance.
Mass resists changes in motion; this idea of **inertial mass** (m = F / a) is developed in 2.22.

head: Change
Effect on acceleration
rows: Double the resultant force, same mass
Halve the resultant force, same mass
Double the mass, same resultant force
Acceleration zero (constant velocity or at rest)

callouts.p: Inversely proportional means a = constant / m, giving a curve. It does not mean a straight line sloping downwards.

core.h: Direction: speeding up, slowing down and turning
core.p: Because force and acceleration are vectors, F = m a also tells you the direction of the acceleration. A resultant force backwards gives a negative acceleration (a deceleration).
bullets: Resultant force **in the direction of motion**: object speeds up.
Resultant force **opposite** to motion: object slows down; a is negative if forwards is positive.
A braking car: braking force 6000 N on a 1500 kg car gives a deceleration of 6000 / 1500 = **4.0 m/s²**.
When asked for a braking force from a negative acceleration, give the **size** of the force and say it acts **backwards**.
A resultant force at right angles to the motion changes the direction; for circular motion this is the centripetal force (2.20 to 2.21).

callouts.p: If a velocity falls from 20 m/s to 8 m/s, a is negative. You can quote the deceleration as a positive number with the word 'deceleration', or as a negative acceleration, but not as a positive acceleration.

core.p: The first and second laws fit together. The first law covers the special case where the resultant force is zero; the second law covers every case.
bullets: F = 0 gives a = 0: at rest or constant velocity (first law).
F not zero gives a = F / m: the velocity changes at a rate set by force and mass.
At **terminal velocity** the resultant force is zero, so acceleration is zero.
Just after a skydiver jumps, air resistance is small so the resultant force is almost equal to the weight, and a is almost g (10 m/s²).
As air resistance increases, the resultant force decreases, so by F = m a the acceleration decreases even though the skydiver is still speeding up.

callouts.t: Decreasing acceleration is not slowing down
callouts.p: If the resultant force gets smaller but stays forwards, the object still speeds up, just more gradually.

core.h: Combining F = m a with the motion equations
core.p: Higher-demand questions often need two or three equations. Acceleration is the 'bridge' quantity: you find it from motion data and use it in F = m a, or find it from F = m a and use it to predict motion.
bullets: From velocity and time: a = (v - u) / t, then F = m a.
From velocity and distance: v² - u² = 2 a x, then F = m a.
From a velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration, then F = m a.
Going the other way: a = F / m, then use v = u + a t or v² - u² = 2 a x to find speed or distance.
Example: a 0.50 kg ball hit from rest to 30 m/s in 0.010 s: a = 30 / 0.010 = 3000 m/s², F = 0.50 x 3000 = 1500 N.
Write down each stage with its equation so method marks can be awarded.

callouts.p: List what you know (u, v, t, x, m, F) and what you need. Pick the equation that contains the unknown and only quantities you already have.

core.h: Weight is a special case of F = m a
core.p: When the only force on an object is its weight, it is in free fall and accelerates at g. Applying F = m a gives W = m g, which is why g is both an acceleration (10 m/s²) and a field strength (10 N/kg).
bullets: In free fall the resultant force = weight, so W = m x g.
a = W / m = m g / m = g, so all masses fall with the same acceleration (ignoring air resistance).
A heavier object has a bigger weight, but also a bigger mass to accelerate, so the acceleration is the same.
Weight, mass and g are covered in detail in 2.16 to 2.18.

callouts.p: Double the mass doubles the weight, but by F = m a the acceleration stays W / m = g.

core.p: F = m a explains many safety and design decisions, and exam questions often set the equation in a real context.
bullets: **Vehicle safety**: a large deceleration means a large force on passengers (F = m a). Crumple zones and air bags increase the stopping time, reducing the deceleration and the force (2.31).
**Lorries**: a large mass means a small acceleration and a small deceleration for a given force, so lorries take longer to speed up and to stop.
**Sports cars**: a powerful engine (large force) and a light body (small mass) both increase acceleration.
**Rockets**: as fuel burns the mass decreases, so with the same thrust the acceleration increases during the launch.
**Lifts**: the resultant of tension and weight decides whether the lift accelerates up, accelerates down or moves at constant speed.

callouts.p: In 'explain' questions quote the relationship: 'a = F / m, so a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration for the same force'.

analogy.p: Push an empty shopping trolley and it shoots forward; push a full one just as hard and it barely speeds up. Push the full one twice as hard and it speeds up twice as quickly. The push is the resultant force, the load is the mass, and how quickly the trolley picks up speed is the acceleration: a = F / m. Where it breaks down: in the supermarket friction from the wheels and floor also acts, so your push is not the resultant force; in F = m a you must subtract friction first. Also the trolley only changes speed while you push, whereas the analogy can make it seem that a push 'gives' a trolley a speed it keeps - in fact the force sets the rate of change of velocity, not the velocity.

terms.d: The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force on it and inversely proportional to its mass: F = m x a.
The single force with the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg); a scalar.
The rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s²; a vector in the direction of the resultant force.
A negative acceleration, when an object slows down because the resultant force acts against its motion.
The unit of force; 1 N is the resultant force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Two quantities are directly proportional if doubling one doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Two quantities are inversely proportional if doubling one halves the other; their product is constant.
A quantity with magnitude and direction, such as force and acceleration.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass.
The forward force from an engine or motor acting on a vehicle.
A force such as friction or air resistance that opposes motion.
The gravitational force on an object, W = m x g.
The slope of a graph; for acceleration against force the gradient equals 1 / mass.
A measure of how difficult it is to change an object's velocity, defined as force divided by acceleration (studied in 2.22).

mistakes.w: Using the driving force in F = m a when friction also acts.
mistakes.r: Use the resultant force: driving force minus resistive forces.

mistakes.w: Using mass in grams, e.g. 500 x 2 = 1000 N.
mistakes.r: Convert to kg: 0.500 kg x 2 m/s² = 1.0 N.

mistakes.w: a = m / F
mistakes.r: a = F / m (acceleration = force divided by mass).

mistakes.w: Doubling the mass doubles the acceleration.
mistakes.r: For the same resultant force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration.

mistakes.w: Acceleration unit given as m/s or N/kg in an answer asking for acceleration.
mistakes.r: Acceleration is measured in m/s² (N/kg is numerically equivalent but m/s² is expected).

mistakes.w: If the resultant force decreases, the object slows down.
mistakes.r: If the resultant force decreases but still acts forwards, the acceleration decreases but the object still speeds up.

mistakes.w: Heavier objects fall faster because they have more weight.
mistakes.r: Weight and mass increase together, so a = W / m = g is the same for all objects in free fall.

mistakes.w: Giving a force without direction when asked for the resultant.
mistakes.r: State size and direction, e.g. 300 N backwards.

mistakes.w: Using the change in velocity in F = m a instead of acceleration.
mistakes.r: First calculate a = (v - u) / t, then use F = m a.

exam.q: Write down the equation that links force, mass and acceleration.
model: force = mass x acceleration (F = m x a)
exam.tip: Word or symbol equation is accepted, but symbols must be the standard ones.

exam.q: What is the unit of acceleration? A m/s B m/s² C N D kg m/s
model: B (m/s²)
exam.tip: 1 N = 1 kg m/s², so m/s² is the unit of a.

exam.q: A resultant force of 120 N acts on a 40 kg box. Calculate its acceleration.
model: a = 3.0 m/s²
exam.tip: Rearrange carefully: force on top.

exam.q: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates at 2.0 m/s². Calculate the resultant force on the car.
exam.tip: Remember the unit N.

exam.q: A resultant force of 18 N gives an object an acceleration of 0.60 m/s². Calculate the mass of the object.
model: m = 30 kg
exam.tip: Mass = force / acceleration.

exam.q: A 250 g trolley is pulled by a resultant force of 0.50 N. Calculate its acceleration.
model: a = 2.0 m/s²
exam.tip: Unit conversion is often a separate mark.

exam.q: The driving force on a motorbike is 1500 N and the resistive forces total 300 N. The motorbike and rider have a mass of 400 kg. Calculate the acceleration.
model: Resultant force = 1500 - 300 = 1200 N
a = 3.0 m/s²
exam.tip: Resultant force first, then F = m a.

exam.q: A loaded lorry and an empty lorry experience the same braking force. Explain which one has the longer braking distance.
model: The loaded lorry has a greater mass
a = F / m, so for the same force its deceleration is smaller
So it takes a greater distance to stop (longer braking distance)
exam.tip: Use the equation in words to justify your answer.

exam.q: A car of mass 900 kg slows from 20 m/s to rest in 5.0 s. Calculate the braking force.
model: a = -4.0 m/s² (deceleration of 4.0 m/s²)
F = 3600 N (acting backwards)
exam.tip: Two equations: find a first.

exam.q: A 0.060 kg tennis ball is served from rest. It reaches 50 m/s after the racket has been in contact for a distance of 0.25 m. Calculate the average force on the ball.
model: v² - u² = 2 a x so 50² - 0 = 2 x a x 0.25
exam.tip: Use v² - u² = 2ax when time is not given.

exam.q: A student investigates how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the resultant force, keeping the mass constant. Describe the relationship they should find and explain how a graph would show it, including what the gradient represents.
model: Acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force
Graph of acceleration against force is a straight line
passing through the origin
Gradient = 1 / mass of the trolley (so a steeper line means a smaller mass)
exam.tip: Proportional needs both 'straight line' and 'through the origin'.

exam.q: A rocket of mass 2.0 x 10^5 kg is launched vertically. The thrust from its engines is 3.0 x 10^6 N. Take g = 10 N/kg. Explain, using calculations, how the rocket's acceleration changes during the first part of the flight as it burns fuel.
model: Resultant force = thrust - weight = 3.0 x 10^6 - 2.0 x 10^6 = 1.0 x 10^6 N upwards
Initial acceleration a = F / m = 1.0 x 10^6 / 2.0 x 10^5 = 5.0 m/s² upwards
As fuel burns the mass of the rocket decreases
So its weight decreases and the resultant force increases (if thrust stays the same)
With a larger resultant force and smaller mass, a = F / m increases, so the acceleration increases
exam.tip: Combine calculation and reasoning; quote a = F / m to justify the change.

worked.q: A 75 kg cyclist pedals with a driving force of 200 N against total resistive forces of 50 N. Calculate the acceleration.
steps: F = m a, so a = F / m.

worked.q: A train of mass 4.0 x 10^5 kg speeds up from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 50 s. Calculate the resultant force on the train.
worked.ans: 1.2 x 10^5 N (120 000 N) in the direction of motion

worked.q: A 1500 kg car travelling at 30 m/s brakes with a constant braking force of 9000 N. Ignoring other resistive forces, calculate the braking distance.
steps: Deceleration a = F / m = 9000 / 1500 = 6.0 m/s² (so a = -6.0 m/s² taking forwards as positive).
Use v² - u² = 2 a x with v = 0 and u = 30 m/s.

phy_edx.1.10.summary: **Inertial mass** tells you how hard it is to change an object's velocity, whether that means starting it moving from rest, speeding it up, slowing it down or changing its direction. It is defined as the **ratio of force over acceleration**, m = F / a, which is just Newton's second law rearranged. The bigger the inertial mass, the bigger the resultant force needed to give the same acceleration, so heavy lorries, full trolleys and oil tankers are slow to start and slow to stop.

core.p: Every object resists changes to its motion. This tendency is called **inertia**, and the quantity that measures how strong it is for a particular object is its **inertial mass**. An object with a large inertial mass needs a large resultant force to change its velocity by a given amount in a given time.
bullets: Inertial mass is a **measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object**.
'Change the velocity' includes **starting from rest**, speeding up, slowing down, stopping and changing direction.
It is measured in **kilograms (kg)**, the same unit as ordinary mass.
It is a **scalar** quantity: it has size but no direction.
It is a property of the object itself, so it does not change if you take the object to the Moon.

callouts.p: Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object (including from rest). It is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration: inertial mass = force / acceleration.

core.h: The defining equation m = F / a
core.p: Newton's second law says resultant force = mass x acceleration (F = m x a). Rearranging gives m = F / a. This is not just algebra: it is the **definition** of inertial mass. If you push something with a known resultant force and measure the acceleration, dividing force by acceleration gives its inertial mass.
bullets: **m = F / a** where m is inertial mass in kg, F is **resultant** force in newtons (N), a is acceleration in m/s².
1 kg is the mass that accelerates at 1 m/s² when a resultant force of 1 N acts on it, so 1 N = 1 kg m/s².
For a fixed force, a = F / m, so **acceleration is inversely proportional to inertial mass**.
Double the mass and the same force gives half the acceleration.
For a fixed acceleration, F = m x a, so the force needed is **directly proportional** to mass.

callouts.p: Examiners reward the exact phrase 'the ratio of force over acceleration'. Write it word for word.

core.h: Why a bigger mass is harder to accelerate
core.p: Think of the same resultant force applied to two trolleys, one empty and one loaded with bricks. The force is shared over more 'stuff' in the loaded trolley, so each part of it gains velocity more slowly. The loaded trolley has the larger inertial mass and the smaller acceleration.
bullets: Same force, larger mass, **smaller acceleration**.
To get the same acceleration with the larger mass, you need a **larger resultant force**.
This is why a full shopping trolley is harder to start moving and harder to stop than an empty one.
Lorries need more powerful engines and stronger brakes than cars for similar accelerations.

fig.cap: The same 20 N resultant force acts on a 2 kg trolley and a 10 kg trolley. Using a = F / m the light trolley accelerates at 10 m/s² while the heavy one only reaches 2 m/s², so the heavy trolley has five times the inertial mass.

core.h: Changing velocity includes starting from rest and changing direction
core.p: Velocity is a vector, so 'changing velocity' means changing speed **or** direction **or** both. Inertial mass resists all of these. An object at rest also has inertia: it resists being set in motion.
bullets: Starting a stationary object moving is a change in velocity from 0 m/s, so inertial mass resists it.
Stopping a moving object is a change in velocity, so a large mass needs a large braking force or a long time.
Turning a corner is a change in direction, so heavy vehicles need a larger centripetal (resultant) force to follow the same curve at the same speed.
A heavy ball is harder to deflect sideways than a light ball at the same speed.

callouts.p: Saying a heavy object is 'harder to move' is too vague. Say it is harder to **change its velocity** (to accelerate or decelerate it).

core.h: Link to Newton's first law and inertia
core.p: Newton's first law says an object stays at rest, or keeps moving at constant velocity, unless a resultant force acts on it. This 'keep doing what you are doing' behaviour is inertia. Inertial mass puts a number on it.
bullets: **Inertia** is the tendency of an object to stay at rest or keep moving at a constant velocity.
**Inertial mass** is the measure of that inertia.
Zero resultant force means zero acceleration, whatever the mass.
A resultant force is needed to change velocity, and the bigger the inertial mass, the bigger that force must be for the same change in the same time.

core.h: Measuring inertial mass from a force-acceleration graph
core.p: If you apply a range of known resultant forces to an object and measure each acceleration, you can plot force (y-axis) against acceleration (x-axis). Because F = m x a, the graph is a **straight line through the origin** and its **gradient equals the inertial mass**.
bullets: Gradient of an F against a graph = F / a = **inertial mass**.
A steeper line means a **larger inertial mass** (more force per unit acceleration).
If a is plotted on the y-axis against F, the gradient is 1 / m instead, so a steeper line then means a smaller mass.
A straight line through the origin shows acceleration is **directly proportional** to force for a fixed mass.

callouts.p: Always read which quantity is on which axis before saying what the gradient means.

fig.cap: Force plotted against acceleration for two objects. Both lines pass through the origin. The gradient of each line is F / a, its inertial mass, so the steeper red line belongs to the object with the larger inertial mass.

core.p: Mass appears in two different equations. In F = m x a it measures resistance to acceleration (inertial mass). In W = m x g it measures how strongly gravity pulls on the object (gravitational mass). Experiments show these two masses are **equal** for every object tested, which is why all objects fall with the same acceleration when air resistance is negligible.
bullets: Inertial mass: from **m = F / a**, resistance to change in velocity.
Gravitational mass: from **W = m x g**, how strongly a gravitational field pulls on the object.
Weight depends on location (g changes); inertial mass does not.
In free fall: a = W / m = (m x g) / m = g, so the mass cancels and every object accelerates at g.
An astronaut in deep space is 'weightless' but still has full inertial mass: a heavy toolbox is still hard to start or stop.

fig.cap: In space there is almost no weight, but pushing a heavy box with a force still produces only a small acceleration, because its inertial mass is unchanged. On Earth the same mass also has a weight W = m x g measured by a balance.

core.p: Examiners often ask you to apply the idea to a real situation. The pattern is always the same: larger inertial mass means a larger force is needed for the same change in velocity, or the same force gives a smaller acceleration or deceleration.
bullets: **Loaded lorry vs car**: the lorry needs a longer braking distance for the same braking force because its deceleration is smaller.
**Oil tanker**: can take several kilometres to stop because its inertial mass is enormous.
**Full vs empty shopping trolley**: the full one is harder to start, stop and steer.
**Rugby**: a heavier player is harder to stop when running at the same velocity.
**Tablecloth trick**: the plates have inertia, so if the cloth is pulled very quickly the small friction force acts for a short time and barely changes the plates' velocity.
**Passengers in a braking car**: their bodies keep moving forward because of their inertia until a seat belt provides a force.

core.h: Resultant force, not just any force
core.p: The F in m = F / a is the **resultant** force. If friction or air resistance acts, you must subtract it from the driving force before using the equation.
bullets: Resultant force = driving force - resistive forces (for forces along one line).
Using the driving force alone gives too high a value of a or too low a value of m.
If the resultant force is zero, the acceleration is zero, so you cannot find inertial mass that way.

callouts.p: Many students divide the engine force by acceleration when friction is also given. Find the resultant force first.

core.p: There are three versions of the equation. Learn the triangle or rearrange algebraically, and always check units.
bullets: m = F / a (inertial mass).
a = F / m (acceleration produced).
F = m x a (force needed).
Convert grams to kilograms (divide by 1000) before calculating.
Convert kN to N (multiply by 1000).
Give answers to sensible significant figures, normally 2 or 3.

core.p: Grade 9 answers use proportion language precisely. Because a = F / m, changes in mass or force scale the acceleration in predictable ways.
bullets: Double the mass, same force: acceleration **halves**.
Double the force, same mass: acceleration **doubles**.
Double both force and mass: acceleration **stays the same**.
Halve the mass, same force: acceleration **doubles**.
If a car tows a trailer of equal mass, the same engine force gives half the acceleration (ignoring friction).

callouts.p: For a fixed resultant force, acceleration is inversely proportional to inertial mass. Using this phrase earns the mark.

analogy.p: Imagine every object has a level of stubbornness about its motion. A small dog on a lead changes direction the instant you tug; a large horse needs a big pull to start, stop or turn. Inertial mass is the stubbornness score, and m = F / a measures it: how much pull you need per unit of change. Where it breaks down: a horse chooses to resist and may pull back, but an object's inertia is not a force and does not push back; it just means the same force produces less acceleration. Also inertia never 'runs out' or tires, unlike an animal.

terms.d: The tendency of an object to stay at rest or to continue moving at a constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.
A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object, including from rest; defined as the ratio of force over acceleration.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; a scalar that does not depend on location.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
The rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s²; a vector.
Speed in a given direction; a vector quantity measured in m/s.
An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force.
The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass: F = m x a.
The unit of force; 1 N gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
The gravitational force acting on an object, W = m x g, measured in newtons.
The force per unit mass in a gravitational field, about 10 N/kg on Earth.
The mass that determines how strongly an object is pulled by gravity; experimentally equal to inertial mass.
Two quantities where doubling one doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Two quantities where doubling one halves the other, so their product is constant.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass.
Negative acceleration; a decrease in velocity over time.

mistakes.w: Inertial mass is how heavy something is.
mistakes.r: Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object; heaviness (weight) is a force measured in newtons.

mistakes.w: A heavy object is harder to move.
mistakes.r: A larger inertial mass needs a larger resultant force to produce the same acceleration (change in velocity).

mistakes.w: Inertial mass = acceleration / force.
mistakes.r: Inertial mass is the ratio of force over acceleration, m = F / a.

mistakes.w: Inertial mass is measured in newtons.
mistakes.r: Inertial mass is measured in kilograms (kg).

mistakes.w: An astronaut in space has no mass so tools are easy to throw.
mistakes.r: In space weight is near zero but inertial mass is unchanged, so the same force is still needed to give the same acceleration.

mistakes.w: Using the driving force in m = F / a when friction acts.
mistakes.r: Use the resultant force (driving force minus resistive forces).

mistakes.w: Objects at rest have no inertia.
mistakes.r: Objects at rest have inertia; inertial mass resists changing velocity from rest.

mistakes.w: Double the mass doubles the acceleration.
mistakes.r: For the same resultant force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration because a = F / m.

mistakes.w: Inertia is a force that keeps things moving.
mistakes.r: Inertia is not a force; it is the tendency to keep the same velocity, measured by inertial mass.

exam.q: State what is meant by inertial mass.
model: A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object.
exam.tip: Use 'change the velocity', not 'move'.

exam.q: Inertial mass is defined as a ratio. State which ratio.
model: Force over (divided by) acceleration, m = F / a.
exam.tip: Give the order clearly: force on top.

exam.q: A resultant force of 1200 N gives a car an acceleration of 1.5 m/s². Calculate the inertial mass of the car.
exam.tip: Write the equation, substitute, then give the unit.

exam.q: A lorry and a car are each acted on by the same resultant braking force. Explain why the lorry takes longer to stop from the same speed.
model: The lorry has a greater (inertial) mass.
So its deceleration is smaller (a = F / m), so it takes longer to reduce its velocity to zero.
exam.tip: Link mass to acceleration with the equation.

exam.q: A trolley has a mass of 2.0 kg. A second identical trolley is stacked on top and the same resultant force is applied. Describe how the acceleration changes.
model: The mass doubles.
The acceleration halves (acceleration is inversely proportional to mass for a constant force).
exam.tip: State the factor, not just 'decreases'.

exam.q: A student plots a graph of resultant force (y-axis) against acceleration (x-axis) for a trolley. State what the gradient represents and describe the shape of the graph.
model: Gradient represents the (inertial) mass of the trolley.
Straight line through the origin.
exam.tip: Gradient = change in y / change in x = F / a.

exam.q: An astronaut on the International Space Station tries to push a heavy equipment box. Explain why the box is still difficult to accelerate even though it appears weightless.
model: The box still has the same (inertial) mass.
A large force is still needed to change its velocity / give it an acceleration (F = m x a).
exam.tip: Separate weight from mass in your answer.

exam.q: A rocket of mass 5000 kg has a thrust of 80 000 N and its weight is 49 000 N. Calculate its initial acceleration.
model: Resultant force = 80 000 - 49 000 = 31 000 N
exam.tip: Always find the resultant force first.

exam.q: Explain the difference between the inertial mass and the weight of an object, and why all objects fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum.
model: Inertial mass measures how difficult it is to change the object's velocity (m = F / a), in kg.
Weight is the gravitational force on the object (W = m x g), in N, and depends on g.
An object with double the mass has double the weight (force),
but also double the inertial mass, so acceleration = W / m = g is the same for all objects.
exam.tip: Show the mass cancelling: a = mg / m = g.

exam.q: Using ideas about inertial mass, explain why a fully loaded supermarket trolley is harder to control than an empty one. Refer to starting, stopping and turning.
model: The loaded trolley has a larger inertial mass.
Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change velocity.
Starting: a larger force is needed to accelerate it from rest at the same rate (F = m x a).
Stopping: for the same force applied, its deceleration is smaller (a = F / m), so it takes longer / further to stop.
Turning: changing direction is a change in velocity, so a larger sideways force is needed to turn it at the same speed.
For the same push, all changes of velocity are smaller / slower, so it is harder to control.
exam.tip: A 6-mark answer should cover each situation and link each to the equation.

worked.q: A force sensor shows a resultant force of 4.8 N acting on a trolley, and a light gate measures its acceleration as 0.60 m/s². Calculate the inertial mass of the trolley.
steps: Write the definition: m = F / a.

worked.q: An empty van of mass 1500 kg accelerates at 2.0 m/s². It is loaded with 1000 kg of goods. Assuming the same resultant force, calculate the new acceleration.
steps: Find the resultant force: F = m x a = 1500 x 2.0 = 3000 N.
worked.ans: The loaded van accelerates at 1.2 m/s², smaller because its inertial mass is larger.

worked.q: A 70 kg astronaut floating in space pushes off a wall with a resultant force of 140 N. Calculate her acceleration and explain why she still needs a force even though she is weightless.
steps: Her weight is close to zero, but her inertial mass is still 70 kg.
Inertial mass measures how difficult it is to change her velocity, so a force is still needed to accelerate her from rest.
worked.ans: a = 2.0 m/s²; she still has inertial mass, so a resultant force is needed to change her velocity.

phy_edx.1.11.summary: **Newton's third law** says that whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are **equal in size and opposite in direction**, and they act on **different objects**. You must be able to apply it to objects in equilibrium (like a book resting on a table) and to collisions. In a collision the two equal and opposite forces act for the same time, so the changes in momentum are equal and opposite, which is exactly why **total momentum is conserved**.

core.p: Forces always come in pairs because a force is an interaction between two objects. If object A pushes or pulls on object B, then B pushes or pulls back on A with a force of the same size in the opposite direction.
bullets: The two forces are **equal in magnitude**.
They are **opposite in direction**.
They act on **two different objects**.
They are the **same type of force** (both contact, both gravitational, both magnetic and so on).
They act **at the same time**: one does not cause the other after a delay.
They act along the same line.

callouts.p: Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.

core.h: Rules for spotting a genuine third-law pair
core.p: A common exam trap is confusing a Newton's third law pair with two balanced forces on the same object. Use the checklist below every time.
bullets: Write each force as 'force of A on B'. Its partner is 'force of B on A'.
If both forces act on the **same object**, they are **not** a third-law pair.
If the forces are **different types** (e.g. weight and normal contact force), they are not a third-law pair.
Third-law forces **never cancel out**, because they act on different objects.
Balanced forces on one object can cancel and give zero resultant force.

head: Feature
Third-law pair
Balanced forces
rows: Book pulls Earth, Earth pulls book
Weight and normal force on a book

callouts.p: The weight of a book and the table's upward push on the book are equal and opposite, but they are NOT a third-law pair: both act on the book and they are different types of force.

core.h: Equilibrium situation: a book on a table
core.p: A book resting on a table is in **equilibrium**: it is stationary, so the resultant force on it is zero. There are two separate third-law pairs in this situation, and it is important to identify them correctly.
bullets: Pair 1 (gravitational): Earth pulls the book down (weight); **the book pulls the Earth up** with an equal force.
Pair 2 (contact): the book pushes down on the table; **the table pushes up on the book** with an equal force (normal contact force).
On the book alone: weight down and normal contact force up are **balanced** (Newton's first law), not a third-law pair.
The Earth does accelerate up towards the book, but its mass is so huge that its acceleration is far too small to notice (a = F / m).

fig.cap: A book resting on a table. The weight W (Earth on book) and the normal contact force R (table on book) both act on the book and balance, so it stays in equilibrium. R pairs with the push P of the book on the table; W pairs with the pull of the book on the Earth.

core.p: In each case below, identify the object you are looking at, list the forces on it, then find each partner force on the other object.
bullets: **Hanging mass on a spring**: the spring pulls up on the mass; the mass pulls down on the spring with an equal force.
**Person leaning on a wall**: the person pushes on the wall; the wall pushes back on the person with an equal force.
**Car moving at constant velocity**: the tyres push backwards on the road; the road pushes forwards on the tyres (this is the driving force). Air resistance balances it on the car.
**Walking**: your foot pushes backward on the ground; the ground pushes you forward with an equal force (friction), which accelerates you.
**Swimming**: hands push water backwards; water pushes the swimmer forwards.

callouts.p: In explanations, always say 'the force of X on Y'. Vague phrases like 'the reaction force' rarely score without saying what acts on what.

core.p: When two objects collide, during the moment of contact each exerts a force on the other. By Newton's third law these forces are **equal and opposite** at every instant, and they act for exactly **the same time** because the contact begins and ends at the same moment for both objects.
bullets: Force of A on B = - (force of B on A).
Contact time is the same for both objects.
The forces are equal, but the **accelerations need not be**: a = F / m, so the lighter object has the larger acceleration.
A small car hitting a lorry feels the same size force as the lorry, but the car's change in velocity is much bigger because its mass is smaller.
The effects (damage, change in velocity) can differ even though the forces are equal.

callouts.p: In a collision the forces are always equal and opposite, but the object with smaller mass has the larger acceleration.

fig.cap: During contact, trolley A pushes B to the right and B pushes A to the left. The forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, act on different trolleys and last for the same contact time.

core.h: From the third law to conservation of momentum
core.p: This is the key link the spec asks for. Force equals rate of change of momentum, so change in momentum = force x time. During a collision both objects feel equal and opposite forces for the same time, so their changes in momentum are equal and opposite. Add them together and the total change in momentum is zero.
bullets: Force on B = F, force on A = -F (third law).
Both act for the same time t.
Change in momentum of B = F x t; change in momentum of A = -F x t.
Total change in momentum = F x t + (-F x t) = **0**.
So **total momentum before = total momentum after** the collision.
This is only true if **no external forces** act (a closed system), e.g. friction is negligible.

callouts.p: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.
Third law: equal and opposite forces; same time; equal and opposite changes in momentum; total change zero; momentum conserved.

core.p: Momentum p = m x v, so it has a direction, the same as the velocity. In conservation problems you must choose a positive direction and give velocities in the opposite direction a negative sign.
bullets: Choose right as positive (or whichever is convenient) and stick with it.
An object moving left has negative momentum.
Two equal masses moving towards each other at equal speeds have a **total momentum of zero**.
If they stick together they stop; if they bounce they separate with equal and opposite velocities.

callouts.p: Forgetting the minus sign for an object moving the opposite way is the most common reason for losing marks in momentum calculations.

core.p: When two objects collide and join, they move off with a common velocity. Use total momentum before = total momentum after to find it.
bullets: m1 x u1 + m2 x u2 = (m1 + m2) x v.
Rearrange: v = (m1 x u1 + m2 x u2) / (m1 + m2).
Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy usually is not; some is transferred to the thermal store and to sound, and work is done deforming the objects.
Example: a railway truck coupling with a stationary truck.

fig.cap: Before: a 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley, total momentum 6 kg m/s. After: they stick together and move at 2 m/s, total momentum still 3 kg x 2 m/s = 6 kg m/s.
