core.h: Explosions and recoil: momentum from zero
core.p: When objects start at rest and push apart (an explosion, a gun firing, two skaters pushing off), the total momentum before is zero, so the total momentum after must also be zero. The pieces move in opposite directions with equal and opposite momenta.
bullets: Before: total momentum = 0.
After: m1 x v1 + m2 x v2 = 0, so m1 x v1 = - m2 x v2.
Newton's third law: the gun pushes the bullet forward, the bullet pushes the gun backward with an equal force for the same time.
The gun **recoils** with a much smaller velocity than the bullet because its mass is much larger.
Rockets: exhaust gases are pushed backwards; the gases push the rocket forwards.

fig.cap: Two skaters at rest push off each other. Each pushes on the other with an equal and opposite force, so total momentum stays zero: the 80 kg skater moves left at 1.5 m/s and the 60 kg skater moves right at 2 m/s.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><marker id='m6' markerWidth='10' markerHeight='10' refX='8' refY='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 Z' fill='#15803d'/></marker></defs><rect x='0' y='0' width='400' height='240' fill='#dbeafe'/><rect x='0' y='190' width='400' height='50' fill='#e9d5ff'/><text x='16' y='222' font-size='12' fill='#5b21b6'>smooth ice</text><circle cx='160' cy='90' r='14' fill='#fde68a' stroke='#92400e' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='160' y1='104' x2='160' y2='150' stroke='#92400e' stroke-width='4'/><line x1='160' y1='150' x2='148' y2='188' stroke='#92400e' stroke-width='4'/><line x1='160' y1='150' x2='172' y2='188' stroke='#92400e' stroke-width='4'/><line x1='160' y1='118' x2='196' y2='118' stroke='#92400e' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='240' cy='96' r='12' fill='#fecaca' stroke='#991b1b' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='240' y1='108' x2='240' y2='150' stroke='#991b1b' stroke-width='4'/><line x1='240' y1='150' x2='230' y2='188' stroke='#991b1b' stroke-width='4'/><line x1='240' y1='150' x2='250' y2='188' stroke='#991b1b' stroke-width='4'/><line x1='240' y1='118' x2='204' y2='118' stroke='#991b1b' stroke-width='4'/><text x='110' y='60' font-size='12' fill='#92400e'>80 kg</text><text x='254' y='60' font-size='12' fill='#991b1b'>60 kg</text><line x1='130' y1='34' x2='60' y2='34' stroke='#15803d' stroke-width='3' marker-end='url(#m6)'/><text x='16' y='22' font-size='12' fill='#15803d'>1.5 m/s</text><line x1='270' y1='34' x2='360' y2='34' stroke='#15803d' stroke-width='3' marker-end='url(#m6)'/><text x='320' y='22' font-size='12' fill='#15803d'>2.0 m/s</text><text x='270' y='176' font-size='12' fill='#1b2540'>total p = 0</text></svg>

core.p: If objects bounce off each other, they still exert equal and opposite forces, so momentum is still conserved. You simply have two unknown velocities after, so a question will give you one of them.
bullets: m1 x u1 + m2 x u2 = m1 x v1 + m2 x v2.
An object that bounces back has a negative velocity after the collision.
A ball bouncing off a wall: the ball's momentum reverses, and the wall (and Earth) gains an equal and opposite momentum that is too small to notice because of its huge mass.

core.h: Why the system must be closed
core.p: Momentum is conserved only when the only significant forces are the internal third-law pairs between the colliding objects. External forces, such as friction from the track or air resistance, add or remove momentum from the system.
bullets: **Closed system**: no external resultant force acts.
Internal forces always come in third-law pairs and cancel when you add up the whole system.
On an air track or smooth ice, friction is negligible, so momentum is very nearly conserved.
In a car crash, friction from the road acts, but during the very short collision it is small compared with the collision forces, so conservation is a good approximation.

analogy.p: Picture two people on skateboards pulling on opposite ends of a rope. However hard one pulls, the rope pulls the other person equally hard in the opposite direction, so the forces are always equal and opposite and last for the same time. The lighter person shoots across faster, but the heavier one also moves, and the total momentum stays zero, so they meet at a point closer to the heavier person. Where it breaks down: in a rope the force is passed through a third object (the rope), whereas Newton's third law pairs act directly between two interacting objects; and people can choose to pull harder, but neither can make their pull bigger than the other's.

terms.d: Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.
The two forces described by Newton's third law: same size, same type, opposite direction, acting on different objects.
A state where the resultant force on an object is zero, so it is stationary or moving at constant velocity.
Forces on the same object that add to give a resultant force of zero.
The force a surface exerts on an object pressing on it, acting at right angles to the surface.
The gravitational force of the Earth on an object, W = m x g.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
Mass x velocity, p = m x v, measured in kg m/s; a vector quantity.
In a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after the event.
A system on which no external resultant force acts, so its total momentum is constant.
An event in which two objects exert forces on each other for a short time when they come into contact.
An event where objects initially at rest push apart; total momentum is zero before and after.
The backward motion of an object, such as a gun, when it pushes another object forward.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as force, velocity and momentum.
The time during which two colliding objects are touching and exerting forces on each other.
A force from outside the system, such as friction or air resistance, that can change the total momentum.

mistakes.w: Weight and the normal contact force on a book are a Newton's third law pair.
mistakes.r: They act on the same object and are different types of force, so they are balanced forces, not a third-law pair.

mistakes.w: Third-law forces cancel out so nothing moves.
mistakes.r: Third-law forces act on different objects, so they cannot cancel each other.

mistakes.w: In a crash between a lorry and a car, the lorry exerts a bigger force.
mistakes.r: The forces are equal and opposite (third law); the car has the larger acceleration because its mass is smaller.

mistakes.w: Every action has a reaction (with no detail).
mistakes.r: State that the forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and act on different objects.

mistakes.w: Momentum is conserved because energy is conserved.
mistakes.r: Momentum is conserved because the forces are equal and opposite and act for the same time, giving equal and opposite changes in momentum.

mistakes.w: Total momentum before an explosion is the momentum of the bullet.
mistakes.r: If everything starts at rest, the total momentum before is zero, so total momentum after is zero.

mistakes.w: Adding momenta without signs for objects moving in opposite directions.
mistakes.r: Momentum is a vector: give velocities in the opposite direction a negative sign.

mistakes.w: Kinetic energy is conserved when objects stick together.
mistakes.r: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; some is transferred to thermal energy and sound.

mistakes.w: The force of the ground on your foot is friction against you, so it slows you down.
mistakes.r: Your foot pushes back on the ground and the ground pushes you forward with an equal and opposite force, which accelerates you.

exam.q: State Newton's third law.
model: Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.
exam.tip: Include 'two objects' or 'each other'.

exam.q: A book rests on a table. The Earth pulls the book downwards with a force of 5 N. State the size and direction of the force that forms a Newton's third law pair with this force, and the object it acts on.
model: 5 N upwards
acting on the Earth (the book pulls the Earth)
exam.tip: The partner is always the same type of force on the other object.

exam.q: Explain why the weight of the book and the normal contact force from the table are not a Newton's third law pair.
model: They both act on the same object (the book).
They are different types of force (gravitational and contact).
exam.tip: Two separate reasons, one per mark.

exam.q: A swimmer pushes backwards on the water with her hands. Use Newton's third law to explain how she moves forward.
model: The water pushes forward on the swimmer
with an equal (and opposite) force, giving her a forward (resultant) force.
exam.tip: Name what acts on what.

exam.q: A small car collides with a large lorry. Compare the forces on the two vehicles and explain why the car's occupants experience a larger change in velocity.
model: The forces are equal (in size) and opposite (Newton's third law).
The car has a smaller mass.
So the car has a larger acceleration/deceleration (a = F / m).
exam.tip: Equal forces, different masses, different accelerations.

exam.q: A 0.010 kg bullet is fired at 400 m/s from a 4.0 kg rifle that is initially at rest. Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle.
model: Total momentum before = 0
Momentum of bullet = 0.010 x 400 = 4.0 kg m/s
Rifle velocity = -4.0 / 4.0 = -1.0 m/s, i.e. 1.0 m/s backwards
exam.tip: State the direction or use a negative sign.

exam.q: A 1200 kg car travelling at 10 m/s collides with a stationary 800 kg car. They lock together. Calculate their velocity just after the collision.
model: Momentum before = 1200 x 10 = 12 000 kg m/s
Combined mass = 2000 kg
exam.tip: Use the combined mass after the collision.

exam.q: State the condition needed for momentum to be conserved in a collision.
model: No external forces act / it is a closed system.
exam.tip: 'No friction' alone may not score; say no external (resultant) force.

exam.q: Two trolleys of equal mass move towards each other at the same speed. They collide and stick together. State their velocity after the collision and explain your answer.
model: Zero / they stop.
Total momentum before is zero because the momenta are equal and opposite, so total momentum after is zero.
exam.tip: Momentum is a vector, so equal and opposite momenta add to zero.

exam.q: Explain, using Newton's third law, why momentum is conserved when two objects collide.
model: During the collision each object exerts a force on the other.
By Newton's third law these forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
The forces act for the same time (the contact time).
Force = change in momentum / time, so change in momentum = force x time.
So the changes in momentum of the two objects are equal and opposite.
The total change in momentum is zero, so total momentum before = total momentum after (if no external forces act).
exam.tip: Follow the chain step by step; examiners award each link.

worked.q: A 3.0 kg trolley moving at 2.0 m/s to the right collides with a 1.0 kg trolley moving at 4.0 m/s to the left. They stick together. Find their velocity after the collision.
steps: Momentum of 3.0 kg trolley = 3.0 x 2.0 = +6.0 kg m/s.
Momentum of 1.0 kg trolley = 1.0 x (-4.0) = -4.0 kg m/s.

worked.q: An 80 kg skater and a 60 kg skater stand at rest on ice and push off each other. The 60 kg skater moves away at 2.0 m/s. Find the velocity of the 80 kg skater and explain using Newton's third law why they move in opposite directions.
steps: Momentum of 60 kg skater = 60 x 2.0 = 120 kg m/s.
Momentum of 80 kg skater must be -120 kg m/s.
Each skater pushes the other with an equal and opposite force (third law), so they accelerate in opposite directions.
worked.ans: 1.5 m/s in the opposite direction to the 60 kg skater

worked.q: A 0.50 kg ball moving at 6.0 m/s hits a stationary 1.5 kg ball. The 0.50 kg ball bounces back at 3.0 m/s. Calculate the velocity of the 1.5 kg ball.
steps: Take the original direction as positive.
Momentum of small ball after = 0.50 x (-3.0) = -1.5 kg m/s.
Momentum of large ball after = 3.0 - (-1.5) = 4.5 kg m/s.
worked.ans: 3.0 m/s in the original direction of the small ball

phy_edx.1.12.summary: **Momentum** is mass x velocity (p = m x v), measured in kg m/s, and because velocity is a vector, momentum is a vector too. In a closed system the total momentum before a collision or explosion equals the total momentum after, which lets you calculate unknown velocities. Newton's second law can be written as **force = change in momentum / time**, F = (mv - mu) / t, which explains why car safety features such as crumple zones, airbags and seat belts protect people: they **increase the time** over which momentum changes, so the **force is smaller**.

core.p: Momentum describes how much 'motion' an object carries. A heavy object moving slowly can have the same momentum as a light object moving fast. You must recall the equation p = m x v.
bullets: **p = m x v**: momentum (kg m/s) = mass (kg) x velocity (m/s).
Unit: **kg m/s** (also written kg m s⁻¹).
Momentum is a **vector**: it has the same direction as the velocity.
An object at rest has **zero momentum**.
Doubling the mass or doubling the velocity doubles the momentum.

callouts.p: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity: momentum = mass x velocity.

core.h: Momentum as a vector and sign conventions
core.p: Since momentum has direction, choose one direction as positive. Anything moving the other way has negative velocity and negative momentum. This matters whenever objects move in opposite directions or bounce back.
bullets: Choose a positive direction (usually right or the initial direction of motion).
An object moving the opposite way has **negative** momentum.
Total momentum is found by **adding** momenta with their signs.
Two objects with equal and opposite momenta have total momentum zero.
A ball that bounces back has a change in momentum bigger than its original momentum.

fig.cap: Taking right as positive, a 1000 kg car at 20 m/s has momentum +20 000 kg m/s and a 4000 kg lorry at 5 m/s moving left has momentum -20 000 kg m/s. They have equal size momenta in opposite directions, so the total momentum is zero.

core.p: In a **closed system** (no external forces), the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. This works for collisions where objects bounce, collisions where objects stick together, and explosions where objects fly apart from rest.
bullets: Total momentum before = total momentum after.
m1 x u1 + m2 x u2 = m1 x v1 + m2 x v2.
Stick together: m1 x u1 + m2 x u2 = (m1 + m2) x v.
Explosion from rest: 0 = m1 x v1 + m2 x v2, so the pieces move in opposite directions.
Momentum is conserved even when kinetic energy is not, because the forces between the objects are equal and opposite (Newton's third law).

callouts.p: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.

core.h: Solving collision problems step by step
core.p: Use the same method every time to avoid sign errors and missing masses.
bullets: 1. Draw a before and after sketch with masses and velocities.
2. Choose a positive direction.
3. Calculate total momentum before (include signs).
4. Write an expression for total momentum after, with the unknown.
5. Set them equal and solve.
6. Give the direction of the answer, not just the size.
Remember the combined mass if objects stick together.

callouts.p: Write 'momentum before = momentum after' explicitly. It often earns a method mark even if arithmetic goes wrong.

fig.cap: Before: a 1500 kg car at 12 m/s runs into the back of a stationary 1000 kg car. After: they move off together. Momentum before 18 000 kg m/s = 2500 kg x v, so v = 7.2 m/s.

core.p: The spec asks you to describe examples of momentum in collisions. In each, identify the objects, the momentum before and after, and what happens to the velocities.
bullets: **Car crashes**: a moving car hits a stationary car; momentum is shared, so both move off more slowly than the first car was going.
**Snooker / pool**: a cue ball hits a stationary ball head-on; the cue ball can stop and the target ball moves off with nearly the same velocity (equal masses).
**Air-track gliders**: used in the lab because friction is almost zero, so momentum conservation can be tested accurately.
**Bullet and block**: a bullet embeds in a block of wood; the block moves off slowly because the combined mass is much larger.
**Football**: a kicked ball gains momentum from the foot, and the foot loses an equal amount.
**Rockets and recoil**: gases pushed backwards gain backward momentum, so the rocket gains equal forward momentum.

core.h: Force as rate of change of momentum
core.p: Newton's second law can be written in a more general form: the resultant force on an object equals its rate of change of momentum. Because a = (v - u) / t, F = m x a becomes F = m x (v - u) / t = (mv - mu) / t.
bullets: **F = (mv - mu) / t**: force (N) = change in momentum (kg m/s) / time (s).
mv = final momentum, mu = initial momentum.
(mv - mu) is the **change in momentum**.
Rearranged: **change in momentum = F x t**.
The same change in momentum can be produced by a **large force for a short time** or a **small force for a long time**.
This equation is given on the equation sheet, but p = m x v must be recalled.

callouts.p: The resultant force on an object is equal to its rate of change of momentum: force = change in momentum / time.

core.p: Grade 9 answers can show where the equation comes from. It is simply F = m x a combined with the definition of acceleration.
bullets: Start with F = m x a.
Acceleration a = (v - u) / t.
Substitute: F = m x (v - u) / t.
Expand: F = (mv - mu) / t.
So force = change in momentum / time taken = rate of change of momentum.

core.h: Large force for short time vs small force for long time
core.p: If a moving object must be brought to rest, its change in momentum is fixed (from mv to zero). The force needed depends only on how long the stop takes. A longer stopping time means a smaller rate of change of momentum, so a smaller force.
bullets: Change in momentum fixed, time increased, **force decreased** (F = change in p / t).
Double the stopping time, halve the force.
Hitting a concrete floor: very short time, very large force, injury.
Landing on a crash mat: longer time, smaller force.
Bending your knees when landing increases the time to stop.

callouts.p: Increasing the time taken for the change in momentum reduces the rate of change of momentum, so it reduces the force.

fig.cap: Two ways of stopping the same object. The force-time curves enclose the same area (same change in momentum), but stopping over a longer time gives a much lower peak force, which is why cushioning reduces injury.

core.p: In a crash, the car and passengers must lose all their momentum. The safety features all work by **increasing the time** taken for this change in momentum, which **decreases the rate of change of momentum** and therefore **decreases the force** on the people inside.
bullets: **Crumple zones**: the front and rear of the car crumple in a controlled way, increasing the collision time; work done deforming them also transfers energy away from the passengers.
**Seat belts**: stretch slightly, so the passenger slows down over a longer time instead of hitting the dashboard or windscreen.
**Airbags**: inflate and then deflate as the passenger presses into them, increasing the time to stop and spreading the force over a larger area.
**Cycle and motorcycle helmets**: crushable foam liner increases the time for the head to stop.
**Crash barriers and gravel traps**: deform or slow the car gradually.

head: Feature
How it increases time
Result
rows: Car front crushes over longer time
Smaller force on car and occupants
Smaller force on head, spread over area

callouts.p: Forces are not absorbed. Say the feature increases the time taken for the change in momentum, so the rate of change of momentum, and hence the force, is reduced.

fig.cap: Safety features in a car. Each one lengthens the time over which the passengers' momentum falls to zero, so the force on them is smaller.

core.h: Calculating force from change in momentum
core.p: Questions usually give mass, initial and final velocities and a time, and ask for the force. Watch out for bounce-back situations where the final velocity is negative.
bullets: Change in momentum = mv - mu.
If an object stops, v = 0, so change in momentum = -mu (a loss of momentum).
If it bounces back, v is negative, so the change in momentum is larger than mu.
Convert milliseconds to seconds: 50 ms = 0.050 s.
The force has direction: a negative answer means the force acts opposite to the initial motion.

callouts.p: Change in momentum in kg m/s divided by time in s gives force in N. Check time is in seconds.

core.p: The same reasoning applies outside cars. Increasing contact time can be used to reduce force (protection) or a longer contact time with a large force can be used to give a bigger change in momentum (performance).
bullets: **Follow-through** in golf, tennis or cricket: keeps the club or bat in contact for longer, so for the same force the ball gets a bigger change in momentum and leaves faster.
**Catching a ball**: moving hands back with the ball increases stopping time, reducing the force on the hands.
**Gymnasts and high-jump mats**: increase landing time.
**Egg drop**: padding increases the time for the egg to stop, reducing the force so it does not break.
**Trampolines and bungee ropes**: stretch over a long time, giving a small force.

analogy.t: Momentum as a bank balance of motion
analogy.p: Think of momentum as money in a 'motion account'. Mass x velocity is the balance, and it can be positive or negative depending on direction. In a collision, objects can only transfer money between their accounts; the total in the system stays the same, just as total momentum is conserved. A force is like a payment rate: removing the same total quickly needs a large rate (big force), removing it slowly needs a small rate (small force), which is what airbags do. Where it breaks down: real money cannot be negative in the same physical sense as moving backwards, and external forces like friction act like a leak to outside the system, which a closed bank account would not have.

terms.d: The product of mass and velocity, p = m x v, measured in kg m/s; a vector.
A quantity with magnitude and direction, such as momentum, velocity and force.
In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.
A system on which no external forces act.
An interaction in which objects exert forces on each other for a short time while in contact.
An event where objects initially at rest are pushed apart; total momentum stays zero.
Final momentum minus initial momentum, mv - mu.
Change in momentum divided by the time taken; equal to the resultant force.
The overall force on an object, equal to its rate of change of momentum.
The velocity of an object at the start of the time interval.
The velocity of an object at the end of the time interval.
A part of a car designed to deform in a collision, increasing the time for the change in momentum and so reducing the force.
A cushion that inflates in a crash, increasing the time for the passenger to stop and spreading the force over a larger area.
A belt that stretches slightly in a crash, increasing the stopping time of the passenger and reducing the force.
The backward movement of an object such as a gun when it pushes another object forward.
A decrease in velocity per unit time; negative acceleration.

mistakes.w: Momentum unit is N or kg/m/s.
mistakes.r: Momentum is measured in kg m/s.

mistakes.w: Momentum = mass x speed with no direction.
mistakes.r: Momentum = mass x velocity and is a vector, so it has direction.

mistakes.w: Airbags absorb the force / absorb the impact.
mistakes.r: Airbags increase the time taken for the change in momentum, so the rate of change of momentum and the force are reduced.

mistakes.w: Crumple zones make the car slow down more.
mistakes.r: Crumple zones increase the time taken to stop, so the deceleration and force are smaller.

mistakes.w: Safety features reduce the change in momentum.
mistakes.r: The change in momentum is the same (from mu to zero); the time increases, so the force decreases.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to add the masses when objects stick together.
mistakes.r: After sticking together, use the combined mass (m1 + m2) with one common velocity.

mistakes.w: Using 50 instead of 0.050 when time is given as 50 ms.
mistakes.r: Convert milliseconds to seconds before using F = (mv - mu) / t.

mistakes.w: Taking the change in momentum of a bouncing ball as m x (v - u) with both velocities positive.
mistakes.r: The rebound velocity is negative, so the change in momentum is m x (v - u) with v negative, giving a larger value.

mistakes.w: Momentum is conserved in all situations.
mistakes.r: Momentum is conserved only in a closed system with no external forces.

exam.q: State the equation linking momentum, mass and velocity.
model: momentum = mass x velocity (p = m x v)
exam.tip: This one must be recalled; it is not on the equation sheet.

exam.q: Calculate the momentum of a 70 kg sprinter running at 9.0 m/s.
model: = 630 kg m/s
exam.tip: Include the unit kg m/s.

exam.q: Explain why momentum is described as a vector quantity.
model: It has both magnitude and direction (because velocity has direction).
exam.tip: Link to velocity.

exam.q: A ball of mass 0.45 kg is kicked from rest and leaves the boot at 20 m/s. The contact time is 0.015 s. Calculate the average force on the ball.
model: Change in momentum = 0.45 x 20 - 0 = 9.0 kg m/s
exam.tip: Write F = (mv - mu) / t first.

exam.q: A 2000 kg truck moving at 3.0 m/s collides with and sticks to a stationary 1000 kg truck. Calculate the velocity of the trucks after the collision.
model: Momentum before = 2000 x 3.0 = 6000 kg m/s
Momentum after = (2000 + 1000) x v
exam.tip: Use the combined mass.

exam.q: State what is meant by a closed system and why it is needed for momentum to be conserved.
model: A system where no external forces act.
External forces would change the total momentum.
exam.tip: Friction and air resistance are typical external forces.

exam.q: A tennis ball of mass 0.060 kg hits a racket at 25 m/s and returns at 35 m/s in the opposite direction. Calculate the change in momentum of the ball.
model: Take initial direction as positive: u = +25 m/s, v = -35 m/s
Change in momentum = 0.060 x (-35) - 0.060 x 25
= -3.6 kg m/s (3.6 kg m/s in the direction of the return)
exam.tip: A bounce adds the two speeds.

exam.q: A 60 kg passenger travelling at 15 m/s is brought to rest by a seat belt in 0.30 s. Calculate the average force on the passenger and state how this would change without the seat belt if the stopping time were 0.030 s.
model: Change in momentum = 60 x 15 = 900 kg m/s
Without seat belt F = 900 / 0.030 = 30 000 N
The force is ten times larger because the time is ten times shorter.
exam.tip: Same change in momentum, different time.

exam.q: Explain how a cycle helmet reduces the risk of head injury in an accident.
model: The foam liner compresses / deforms on impact.
This increases the time taken for the head to stop (change momentum).
So the rate of change of momentum is smaller, so the force on the head is smaller.
exam.tip: Always mention time, rate of change of momentum and force.

exam.q: Explain how crumple zones, seat belts and airbags reduce injuries to passengers in a car crash. Use ideas about momentum in your answer.
model: In a crash the passengers' momentum must decrease to zero; the change in momentum is the same whatever happens.
Force = change in momentum / time (rate of change of momentum).
Crumple zones deform, increasing the time taken for the car to stop.
Seat belts stretch slightly, increasing the time for the passenger to stop.
Airbags inflate and compress, increasing the stopping time and spreading the force over a larger area.
A longer time means a smaller rate of change of momentum, so a smaller force on the passengers, so fewer injuries.
exam.tip: Name each feature and link each to increased time, then to smaller force.

worked.q: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 25 m/s crashes into a wall and stops in 0.080 s. Calculate the average force on the car. A car with a better crumple zone stops in 0.20 s. Calculate the new force.
steps: Change in momentum = mv - mu = 1200 x 0 - 1200 x 25 = -30 000 kg m/s.
Size of force = 375 000 N (opposite to motion).
Increasing the time reduces the force.
worked.ans: 375 000 N without, 150 000 N with the better crumple zone

worked.q: A 5.0 kg firework at rest explodes into two pieces. A 2.0 kg piece flies east at 15 m/s. Find the velocity of the other piece.
steps: Momentum of 2.0 kg piece = 2.0 x 15 = +30 kg m/s (east positive).

worked.q: A 0.16 kg cricket ball travelling at 30 m/s is caught. The fielder's hands bring it to rest in 0.12 s. Calculate the force on the hands and explain why moving the hands back with the ball reduces this force.
steps: Change in momentum = 0.16 x 30 = 4.8 kg m/s.
Moving the hands back increases the time for the change in momentum.
Since F = change in momentum / time, a longer time gives a smaller force.
worked.ans: 40 N; moving hands back increases the stopping time, so reduces the rate of change of momentum and the force.

phy_edx.1.13.summary: Your **reaction time** is the time between a **stimulus** (seeing, hearing or feeling something) and your **response** (moving a muscle). Edexcel expects you to describe how to measure it, most often with the **ruler drop test** or a **computer-based test**, and to recall that typical human reaction times are about **0.2 s to 0.9 s**. You must be able to turn a ruler-drop distance into a time using free-fall ideas, explain why repeats and averages are needed, and say what factors (tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions) make reaction times longer.

core.p: A reaction time is how long your nervous system takes to detect a stimulus, process it in the brain and send a signal to your muscles so you respond. Nothing is 'instant': signals need time to travel along neurones and the brain needs time to decide.
bullets: **Stimulus**: the change you detect, e.g. a ruler starting to fall, a light turning on, a sound.
**Response**: the action you make, e.g. closing your fingers, pressing a button.
Reaction time = time of response minus time of stimulus.
It is measured in **seconds (s)**, usually quoted to 2 or 3 decimal places.
Reaction time is the main reason a driver has a **thinking distance** (covered in 2.28 to 2.30).

callouts.p: The time taken between a person detecting a stimulus and responding to it.

fig.cap: A reaction is a chain: the eye detects the stimulus, the brain processes it, then muscles respond. The total time from stimulus to response is the reaction time, typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s.

core.p: Edexcel expects you to recall typical results. For a simple, alert person waiting for one expected stimulus, reaction times are short; in real situations such as driving, where you must notice, decide and move a foot, they are longer.
bullets: Typical human reaction time: **0.2 s to 0.9 s**.
A ruler drop test usually gives about **0.15 s to 0.3 s** for an alert student.
A driver's reaction time is often taken as about **0.7 s** in calculations, longer if tired or distracted.
Values below about 0.1 s in a test usually mean the person **anticipated** (guessed) rather than reacted.
Reaction times differ from person to person and change for the same person through the day.

callouts.p: Typical reaction time is between **0.2 s and 0.9 s**. Answers outside this range in an estimate question should make you check your working.

core.p: This is the classic school method. One person drops a metre rule and the other catches it as soon as they see it move. The further the ruler falls before it is caught, the longer the reaction time.
bullets: The **catcher** sits with their forearm resting on the edge of a table so only the hand moves.
The **tester** holds a 30 cm or metre rule vertically, with the **zero mark** level with the top of the catcher's thumb.
The catcher's thumb and finger are apart, either side of the ruler but **not touching** it.
The tester lets go **without warning**, at a random moment.
The catcher closes their fingers as fast as possible.
Read the distance on the ruler at the **top of the thumb** where it was caught.
Repeat many times (e.g. 10), discard anomalies and calculate a **mean** distance.
Convert the distance into a time using a conversion table or the free-fall equations.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward: zero at the thumb, drop without warning, read distance at top of thumb, repeat and take a mean, convert distance to time.

core.h: Why the ruler drop works: free fall
core.p: Once released, the ruler falls freely, accelerating at g = 10 m/s² (air resistance is negligible for a ruler over a short distance). Because its acceleration is known and constant, the distance it falls depends only on how long it falls for, which is the reaction time.
bullets: Initial velocity u = 0 m/s because the ruler starts at rest.
Acceleration a = g = 10 m/s² (Edexcel uses g = 10 N/kg).
Step 1: use **v² − u² = 2 × a × x** to find the ruler's speed v when caught.
Step 2: use **a = (v − u) / t**, rearranged to **t = (v − u) / a**, to find the time.
Shortcut result: t = √(2x / g). With g = 10, x = 0.20 m gives t = 0.20 s.
The distance fallen is **not proportional** to the time: double the time gives four times the distance, because the ruler is speeding up.

callouts.p: Convert the ruler reading from cm to m before using the equations. 18 cm = 0.18 m.

fig.cap: Distance a dropped ruler falls against reaction time (x = ½gt² with g = 10 m/s²). The curve gets steeper because the ruler accelerates, so a small extra reaction time adds a lot of extra distance.

core.h: Conversion table for the ruler drop
core.p: Instead of calculating each time, a conversion table can be used. These values come from the free-fall equations with g = 10 m/s².
bullets: The table shows the distances get further apart for equal time steps, because the ruler is accelerating.
A ruler drop test cannot measure reaction times longer than the time the ruler takes to fall its full length: about 0.25 s for a 30 cm ruler, about 0.45 s for a 1 m rule.
This is why a **metre rule** gives a wider range than a 30 cm ruler.

core.p: A computer program changes the screen (for example from red to green) at a random moment and starts an electronic timer. The person presses a key or clicks the mouse as soon as they see the change, and the computer records the time gap.
bullets: The stimulus appears at a **random** time so the person cannot anticipate it.
Timing is done **electronically**, so it is more precise (often to 0.001 s) than reading a ruler.
It removes the human error of the tester and of reading the ruler scale.
Repeat several times and calculate a mean.
Some delay comes from the equipment itself (keyboard or screen lag), which is a **systematic error** adding a small amount to every reading.
Similar tests use a **sound** stimulus (a beep) or a **touch** stimulus to compare senses.

core.p: Any method needs a clear start signal (the stimulus) and a clear stop signal (the response), with a timer between them.
bullets: **Light and switch**: a lamp switches on and a timer starts; the person presses a switch that stops the timer.
**Sound and button**: a buzzer sounds and the person presses a button.

**Chain reaction**: a group holds hands in a line; the first squeezes, each person squeezes the next, and the total time divided by the number of people gives an average reaction time. This uses a stopwatch, so it is less precise.
**Stopwatch alone** is poor for a single reaction because the person timing has their own reaction time of similar size to the thing being measured.

callouts.p: Do not suggest timing a single reaction with a hand-held stopwatch: the timer's own reaction time (about 0.2 s) is as big as the result.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to evaluate methods. Think about precision, sources of error and how easily the test can be repeated.
bullets: Electronic timing reduces human timing error.
Random start reduces anticipation in all methods.
Ruler test is cheap and needs no electricity, but readings are only to the nearest 0.5 cm or so.

head: Feature
Ruler drop
Computer test
rows: Reading at thumb, ruler not vertical, hand moving
Yes, using g or a table

core.h: Making the test fair and the results reliable
core.p: Reaction time varies a lot from one try to the next, so a single result is not trustworthy. Good practice reduces random error and keeps the comparison fair.
bullets: **Repeat** each test many times and calculate a **mean**; this reduces the effect of random errors.
Ignore **anomalous** results (for example a catch at 0 cm, which means the person guessed).
Keep **control variables** the same: same hand (dominant), same ruler, same starting gap between thumb and finger, same height of fingers.
The same tester should drop the ruler each time and **vary the delay** before dropping.
Rest the forearm on a table so the arm cannot move down to catch the ruler.
Allow a few **practice** goes first, because people improve with practice.

callouts.p: Repeating and averaging makes results more **reliable** (repeatable). Using electronic timing makes them more **accurate and precise**.

core.p: Anything that slows the detection of a stimulus, the processing in the brain, or the signal to the muscles increases reaction time. This links directly to driving and thinking distance.
bullets: **Tiredness** increases reaction time.
**Alcohol** and many **drugs** (including some medicines) increase reaction time.
**Distractions** (mobile phone, loud music, talking to passengers) increase reaction time because attention is split.
**Age** can affect it: older people often react more slowly.
**Caffeine** can slightly decrease reaction time for a short period.
**Practice** can decrease reaction time in a test.
The type of stimulus matters: people usually react slightly faster to sound or touch than to sight.

callouts.p: Longer reaction time means the car travels further at constant speed before braking starts, so the **thinking distance** increases.

core.p: You may be asked to plan an investigation, for example into whether caffeine or distraction changes reaction time. Use the scientific method.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the factor changed, e.g. distraction (none / talking / music).
**Dependent variable**: the reaction time (or ruler distance).
**Control variables**: same person, same hand, same ruler, same time of day, same tester.
Take repeats for each condition and compare **means**.
Present results in a **bar chart** if the independent variable is categoric.
Draw a conclusion only if the difference between means is bigger than the spread (range) of the repeats.

core.h: Why reaction time matters in real life
core.p: Reaction time limits how quickly anyone can start to respond to danger. At high speed, even a short reaction time means a large distance travelled before anything happens.
bullets: At 30 m/s, a reaction time of 0.7 s means the car travels 30 × 0.7 = 21 m before the brakes are applied.
Doubling the reaction time doubles the thinking distance (speed is constant during the reaction).
Sports starts (sprint races) treat a reaction under 0.1 s as a false start, because humans cannot genuinely react that fast.

analogy.t: Reaction time is like a delivery service
analogy.p: Your eye is the shop taking an order (stimulus), your brain is the warehouse working out what to send, and your muscles are the customer receiving the parcel (response). The reaction time is the delivery time, and tiredness, alcohol or distractions are like traffic jams that make every delivery slower. Where it breaks down: a real delivery is one trip, but in your body the signal is electrical and chemical, travels along neurones in fractions of a second, and much of the delay is the brain processing rather than travel.

terms.d: The time between a person detecting a stimulus and responding to it.
A change in the surroundings that is detected, e.g. a light, sound or moving object.
The action made as a result of the stimulus, e.g. gripping a ruler.
A method where a ruler is dropped without warning and the distance it falls before being caught is used to find reaction time.
Motion where the only force acting is weight, so the object accelerates at g.
The force per kilogram on a mass, 10 N/kg at the Earth's surface; equal to the free-fall acceleration of 10 m/s².
The total of a set of repeat readings divided by the number of readings.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others and is left out of the mean.
Unpredictable variation in readings, reduced by repeating and averaging.
An error that shifts every reading by the same amount, e.g. computer lag.
A variable kept the same so that the test is fair.
Responding because you guess the stimulus is coming, giving a falsely short reaction time.
How closely repeated measurements agree; electronic timers give more precise times.
The distance travelled during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied.

mistakes.w: The ruler falls at a constant speed so distance is proportional to time.
mistakes.r: The ruler accelerates at 10 m/s², so distance is proportional to time squared; use v² − u² = 2ax then t = v / a.

mistakes.w: Measure the reaction time once with the ruler.
mistakes.r: Repeat several times, remove anomalies and calculate a mean.

mistakes.w: The tester counts down before dropping the ruler.
mistakes.r: Drop the ruler without warning at a random time so the catcher cannot anticipate.

mistakes.w: Use 18 cm directly in the equation.
mistakes.r: Convert to metres first: 0.18 m.

mistakes.w: Reaction time is about 2 to 3 seconds.
mistakes.r: Typical reaction time is 0.2 s to 0.9 s.

mistakes.w: Time a single reaction with a stopwatch.
mistakes.r: A stopwatch adds the timer's own reaction time; use a ruler drop or electronic timer.

mistakes.w: Alcohol makes your reactions faster/more relaxed.
mistakes.r: Alcohol increases reaction time (slower reactions).

mistakes.w: Repeating makes the result more accurate.
mistakes.r: Repeating and finding a mean makes the result more reliable and reduces the effect of random errors.

exam.q: State a typical value for human reaction time.
model: Any value from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
exam.tip: Always include the unit s.

exam.q: State two factors that can increase a person's reaction time.
model: Tiredness / fatigue.
Alcohol, drugs or distractions (e.g. using a mobile phone).
exam.tip: Speed of the car is NOT a factor affecting reaction time.

exam.q: Describe how a ruler can be used to measure a student's reaction time.
model: Hold the ruler vertically with zero level with the top of the student's thumb, fingers apart.
Drop the ruler without warning.
Student catches it; read the distance at the top of the thumb.
Repeat and calculate a mean distance; convert distance to time using a table or equation.
exam.tip: Mention both 'without warning' and 'repeat and mean'.

exam.q: Explain why the tester should vary the time before releasing the ruler.
model: So the catcher cannot predict/anticipate when the ruler will drop.
Otherwise measured reaction time is too short / not a true reaction.
exam.tip: Use the word anticipate.

exam.q: A ruler falls 0.20 m before being caught. Calculate the reaction time. Use g = 10 m/s².
exam.tip: Two-step method using equations from the sheet.

exam.q: Suggest one advantage of using a computer test rather than a ruler drop test.
model: Electronic timing is more precise / removes human error in reading the ruler / gives time directly.
exam.tip: Give a specific reason, not just 'more accurate'.

exam.q: A student records ruler distances of 15 cm, 17 cm, 2 cm and 16 cm. Explain which result should be ignored and calculate the mean of the rest.
model: 2 cm is anomalous (student probably anticipated).
exam.tip: Say why it is anomalous, not just that it is.

exam.q: Explain why a 30 cm ruler cannot measure a reaction time of 0.4 s.
model: In 0.4 s the ruler would fall x = ½ × 10 × 0.4² = 0.8 m.
This is longer than the ruler, so it would hit the ground / not be caught.
exam.tip: Show the calculated fall distance.

exam.q: Explain why a longer reaction time is dangerous for a car driver.
model: Car travels at constant speed during the reaction time.
So thinking distance (and stopping distance) increases, greater chance of hitting an obstacle.
exam.tip: Link reaction time to thinking distance.

exam.q: A student wants to find out whether listening to music affects reaction time. Describe a plan for the investigation.
model: Independent variable: music on or off; dependent variable: reaction time.
Use ruler drop test (or computer test) with zero at top of thumb, dropped without warning.
Control variables: same person/hand/ruler/tester/time of day.
Take at least 5 to 10 repeats in each condition.
Remove anomalies, calculate mean for each condition and convert to time.
Compare means; conclude music has an effect only if difference is larger than the spread of results.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a logical sequence: variables, method, control, repeats, analysis, conclusion.

worked.q: A ruler falls 0.45 m before it is caught. Calculate the reaction time (g = 10 m/s²).
Student A's ruler readings are 12 cm, 14 cm, 13 cm. Student B's are 22 cm, 20 cm, 21 cm. Who reacts faster and by how much (in s)?
worked.ans: Student A reacts faster, by about 0.04 s.

worked.q: A driver with a reaction time of 0.6 s is travelling at 25 m/s. After using a phone, her reaction time becomes 1.2 s. Find the increase in the distance travelled before she brakes.
steps: During the reaction the speed is constant, so distance = speed × time.

phy_edx.1.14.summary: The **stopping distance** of a vehicle is the **thinking distance** (travelled during the driver's reaction time) **plus** the **braking distance** (travelled while the brakes slow the car to rest). Thinking distance depends on **speed** and the driver's **reaction time**, which is made longer by tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions. Braking distance depends on **speed**, **mass**, the **state of the brakes**, the **state of the road** and the **friction between tyres and road**. At grade 9 you must explain each factor using forces, deceleration and energy, not just list it.

core.h: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
core.p: When a driver sees a hazard, the car does not start slowing immediately. First the driver must react, during which the car keeps going at its original speed. Then the brakes act and the car decelerates to rest. The two distances add together.
bullets: **Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance**.
Thinking distance happens at **constant speed** (no braking yet).
Braking distance happens while the car **decelerates**.
All three are distances, measured in metres (m).
Any factor that increases either part increases the total stopping distance.

callouts.p: The total distance travelled from when the driver sees a hazard to when the vehicle stops: the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance.

core.p: Thinking distance is the distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time. Because the speed is constant during this time, it can be found from distance = speed × time.
bullets: **Thinking distance = speed × reaction time**.
Depends on **speed** of the vehicle and **reaction time** of the driver only.
Thinking distance is **directly proportional** to speed: double the speed, double the thinking distance (if reaction time stays the same).
It does **not** depend on the road surface, the brakes, the tyres or the mass of the car.
Typical reaction time used in calculations: about **0.7 s** (range 0.2 s to 0.9 s).

callouts.p: The distance travelled by the vehicle during the driver's reaction time.

core.p: Braking distance is the distance the vehicle travels after the brakes are applied until it stops. The brakes create a friction force that decelerates the car.
bullets: Depends on: **speed**, **mass** of the vehicle, **condition of the brakes**, **condition of the road**, and **friction between the tyres and the road** (tyre tread).
It does **not** depend on the driver's reaction time.
Larger braking force gives larger deceleration (F = m × a) and a shorter braking distance.
Braking distance increases faster than speed: doubling speed roughly **quadruples** braking distance, because kinetic energy depends on v².

callouts.p: The distance travelled by the vehicle under the braking force, from when the brakes are applied until it stops.

core.h: Speed and stopping distances on a velocity-time graph
core.p: A velocity-time graph of a car stopping shows both parts clearly. The area under a velocity-time graph equals distance travelled.
bullets: Flat section: constant velocity during the reaction time; area of the rectangle = **thinking distance**.
Sloping section: steady deceleration while braking; area of the triangle = **braking distance**.
A longer reaction time makes the flat section longer, so more thinking distance.
A smaller braking force makes the slope less steep, so the triangle is longer and has a bigger area.

callouts.p: Thinking distance = v × t(reaction). Braking distance = ½ × v × t(braking) for a straight-line slope down to zero.

core.h: How the brakes work: forces and energy
core.p: When the driver presses the brake pedal, brake pads are pushed against discs on the wheels. Friction between pads and discs slows the wheels, and friction between the tyres and the road then provides the backwards force on the car.
bullets: Work is done by the friction force: **work done = force × distance**.
The car's **kinetic energy store** decreases and the **thermal energy store** of the brakes increases (they get hot), with some energy also dissipated to the surroundings.
To stop, all the kinetic energy must be transferred: **braking force × braking distance = ½ × m × v²**.
So braking distance = ½mv² / F: bigger mass or speed means more energy to remove, so a longer distance for the same force.
Very hard braking can overheat the brakes, reducing their friction (brake fade), or lock the wheels so the car skids.

callouts.p: Braking transfers energy from the **kinetic store** of the vehicle to the **thermal store** of the brakes by work done by friction.

core.p: Speed affects **both** parts of the stopping distance, which is why speed is the most important factor.
bullets: Thinking distance: at higher speed the car travels further during the same reaction time (distance = speed × time), so it is proportional to speed.
Braking distance: kinetic energy = ½mv², so doubling speed gives four times the kinetic energy; with the same braking force the car needs four times the distance.
Speed limits are lower near schools and in towns for this reason.
At 30 mph: 9 m + 14 m = 23 m. At 70 mph: 21 m + 75 m = 96 m.

callouts.p: Braking distance is NOT proportional to speed. Doubling speed roughly quadruples braking distance.

core.p: A heavier vehicle (more passengers, luggage, or a lorry) is harder to stop.
bullets: More mass means more **kinetic energy** at the same speed, so more work must be done by the brakes.
For the same braking force, deceleration is smaller because **a = F / m**.
Smaller deceleration means a **longer braking distance**.
Mass does **not** affect thinking distance (the driver's reaction does not depend on the car's mass).

core.p: Brakes rely on friction between the brake pads and discs. If that friction is reduced, the braking force is smaller.
bullets: **Worn** brake pads or discs produce less friction, so a smaller braking force.
Brakes that are **wet**, **oily** or **overheated** also grip less.
Smaller braking force means smaller deceleration and a **longer braking distance**.
Regular servicing keeps brakes effective.

core.h: Factor: state of the road and friction between tyres and road
core.p: The braking force on the car ultimately comes from friction between the tyres and the road surface. If there is less grip, the car cannot decelerate as quickly and may skid.
bullets: **Wet** roads: a layer of water between tyre and road reduces friction.
**Icy** roads: very low friction, braking distance can be up to about ten times longer.
**Loose gravel, leaves, oil or mud** reduce friction.
**Worn tyres** (low tread depth) cannot push water away through the tread grooves, so grip falls on wet roads; the legal minimum tread depth in the UK is 1.6 mm.
Under-inflated or poor-quality tyres also reduce grip.

Less friction means smaller maximum braking force, smaller deceleration and **longer braking distance**; if the brakes are applied too hard the wheels **lock** and the car **skids**, which reduces control.

callouts.p: Full-mark answers follow the chain: wet road → less friction between tyres and road → smaller braking force → smaller deceleration → longer braking distance.

core.p: Reaction time affects only the thinking distance. Anything that slows the driver noticing, deciding or moving their foot increases the reaction time.
bullets: **Tiredness** (fatigue): slower processing by the brain.
**Alcohol**: slows the nervous system and impairs judgement; illegal above the drink-drive limit.
**Drugs**: illegal drugs and some prescription or over-the-counter medicines (e.g. some that cause drowsiness) increase reaction time.
**Distractions**: using a mobile phone, adjusting the radio or satnav, talking to passengers, eating; attention is not on the road.
**Age** and **poor visibility** (fog, darkness) can also delay noticing a hazard.
Longer reaction time → car travels further at constant speed → longer **thinking distance** → longer stopping distance.

callouts.p: Alcohol, drugs, tiredness and distractions affect THINKING distance. Ice, worn tyres and worn brakes affect BRAKING distance.

core.p: Use this to check which part of the stopping distance each factor changes.
bullets: Only **speed** appears in both columns.
Weather (rain, ice, fog) can affect both: fog lengthens reaction (harder to see), rain and ice lengthen braking.

head: Factor
Thinking distance
Braking distance
rows: Longer reaction time (tired, alcohol, drugs, distraction)

core.p: Understanding stopping distances explains many road safety rules.
bullets: Keep a **safe gap** to the car in front: at least a two-second gap in good conditions, more in rain or ice.
**Speed limits** cut both thinking and braking distances near schools and housing.
Laws against **drink-driving** and **using hand-held mobile phones** reduce reaction times.
Minimum **tyre tread** depth and **MOT tests** (brakes) keep braking distances short.
Drivers should slow down in bad weather because braking distances increase.

analogy.t: Stopping a car is like catching a falling plate
analogy.p: First you have to notice the plate slipping and decide to move (thinking time, during which it keeps falling at its own pace), then your hands slow it down (braking). If you are distracted you notice later, and the plate gets further before your hands even move. If your hands are slippery (wet road) or the plate is heavier (more mass), it takes longer to bring it to rest. Where it breaks down: the plate speeds up as it falls, whereas a car's speed stays constant during thinking time, and a car's braking force comes from friction between tyres and road, not from muscles.

terms.d: The sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance.
The distance travelled during the driver's reaction time, at constant speed.
The distance travelled under the braking force from when the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops.
The time between the driver seeing a hazard and applying the brakes.
The friction force that decelerates the vehicle when the brakes are applied.
Negative acceleration; the rate at which velocity decreases.
A force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact, e.g. tyres and road, brake pads and discs.
Energy in the kinetic store of a moving object: KE = ½ × m × v².
Energy transferred when a force moves through a distance: work done = force × distance.
The store that increases when the brakes heat up during braking.
Grooves in a tyre that push water away so the tyre keeps contact with the road; legal minimum depth 1.6 mm.
Sliding of the tyres over the road when the wheels lock because the braking force needed exceeds the friction available.
Anything that takes the driver's attention from the road, e.g. using a mobile phone, increasing reaction time.
Two quantities where doubling one doubles the other, e.g. thinking distance and speed.

mistakes.w: A wet road increases the thinking distance.
mistakes.r: A wet road reduces friction and increases the braking distance only.

mistakes.w: Alcohol increases the braking distance.
mistakes.r: Alcohol increases reaction time and so increases the thinking distance.

mistakes.w: Stopping distance = thinking distance × braking distance.
mistakes.r: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

mistakes.w: Doubling speed doubles the braking distance.
mistakes.r: Doubling speed doubles thinking distance but roughly quadruples braking distance (KE ∝ v²).

mistakes.w: Worn tyres have less friction so the car goes faster.
mistakes.r: Worn tyres give less grip/friction with the road, so a smaller braking force, smaller deceleration and longer braking distance.

mistakes.w: Brakes turn kinetic energy into heat energy.
mistakes.r: Work done by friction transfers energy from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes.

mistakes.w: A heavier car stops faster because it has more grip.
mistakes.r: More mass means more kinetic energy and smaller deceleration for the same braking force, so a longer braking distance.

mistakes.w: Being tired makes it take longer to brake.
mistakes.r: Being tired increases the reaction time, so the car travels further before the brakes are applied (longer thinking distance).

exam.q: State the equation linking stopping distance, thinking distance and braking distance.
model: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
exam.tip: Words are fine; symbols are not given on the sheet.

exam.q: State two factors that affect the thinking distance of a car.
model: Speed of the car.
Reaction time of the driver (or a factor affecting it, e.g. tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions).
exam.tip: Road conditions are not accepted here.

exam.q: State two factors, other than speed, that affect the braking distance of a car.
model: Any two of: mass of car, condition of brakes, condition of road (wet/icy), condition of tyres / friction between tyres and road.
exam.tip: Be specific: 'worn tyres' rather than just 'tyres'.

exam.q: Describe how using a mobile phone affects the stopping distance of a car.
model: Distraction increases the driver's reaction time.
So thinking distance (and therefore stopping distance) increases.
exam.tip: Name the part of stopping distance that changes.

exam.q: A car travels at 20 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.7 s. Calculate the thinking distance.
model: distance = speed × time = 20 × 0.7
exam.tip: Speed is constant during reaction time.

exam.q: The thinking distance is 12 m and the braking distance is 24 m. Calculate the stopping distance.
exam.tip: Simple addition, but give the unit.

exam.q: Explain why an icy road increases the stopping distance of a car.
model: Ice reduces friction between the tyres and the road.
So the maximum braking force is smaller / the car decelerates less (or skids).
So braking distance increases, so stopping distance increases.
exam.tip: Thinking distance does not change; say so if asked to compare.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of energy, why a loaded van has a longer braking distance than the same van empty, at the same speed.
model: Loaded van has greater mass so more kinetic energy (KE = ½mv²).
Brakes must do more work to transfer this energy (work = force × distance).
With the same braking force, a greater distance is needed.
exam.tip: Link KE, work done and distance.

exam.q: Describe the energy transfer that takes place when a car brakes to a stop.
model: Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the car.
To the thermal store of the brakes (and surroundings) by work done by friction.
exam.tip: Use 'store' and 'work done by friction'.

exam.q: Explain how the speed of a car, the condition of the driver and the condition of the road affect the stopping distance of the car. Refer to thinking distance and braking distance in your answer.
model: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
Higher speed increases thinking distance as more distance is covered during the reaction time (proportional to speed).
Higher speed also increases braking distance (more KE to remove, about four times when speed doubles).
Tiredness, alcohol, drugs or distractions increase reaction time so increase thinking distance only.
Wet, icy or gravel road reduces friction between tyres and road so increases braking distance only.
Smaller friction means smaller braking force and smaller deceleration; risk of skidding.
exam.tip: Structure: define, then speed, then driver, then road; say which part each factor changes.

worked.q: A car travels at 30 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.6 s. The car then decelerates uniformly to rest in 5.0 s. Calculate the stopping distance.
steps: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time = 30 × 0.6 = 18 m.
Braking distance = area of triangle on v-t graph = ½ × 30 × 5.0 = 75 m.

worked.q: A car of mass 1200 kg travels at 20 m/s. The braking force is 6000 N. Calculate the braking distance.
steps: Work done by brakes = KE lost, so F × d = 240 000.

worked.q: The driver in the first example has drunk alcohol, raising her reaction time to 1.2 s. The road is dry. Find the new stopping distance and explain which part changed.
steps: Braking distance is unchanged at 75 m because alcohol does not affect the brakes or road.
worked.ans: 111 m; only the thinking distance increased (by 18 m).

phy_edx.1.15.summary: A vehicle or person that stops very quickly has a **large deceleration**, and by **F = m × a** a large deceleration needs a **large force**. Large forces on the body cause serious injury, so road-safety design aims to **increase the time** (and distance) over which a collision happens, which **reduces the deceleration and the force**. Edexcel expects you to explain these dangers and to **estimate** realistic decelerations and forces for typical road situations using typical masses, speeds and stopping times or distances; at Higher tier you link this to **force = rate of change of momentum**.

core.p: Deceleration is how quickly velocity decreases. Newton's second law says the resultant force needed is F = m × a, so stopping something quickly (large deceleration) needs a large force. In a crash, that force acts on the car and on the people in it.
bullets: Large deceleration → **large force** on the vehicle and the occupants.
Large forces can **break bones**, damage the neck (whiplash) and injure internal organs.
Because of **inertia**, the body and its organs tend to keep moving when the car stops suddenly; the brain can hit the inside of the skull.
Large decelerations when braking hard can **lock the wheels**, causing a **skid** and loss of control, and can **overheat the brakes**.
The faster the vehicle and the shorter the stopping time, the larger the deceleration and force.

callouts.p: Large deceleration means large force (F = m × a), and large forces cause injury. Increasing the stopping time reduces the deceleration and so reduces the force.

core.p: All the estimates on this point use equations from the motion topic. Choose the one that matches the information you have.
bullets: **a = (v − u) / t**: deceleration from a change of velocity and the time taken.
**v² − u² = 2 × a × x**: deceleration from a change of velocity and the stopping distance.
**F = m × a**: force from mass and deceleration.
Higher tier: **F = (mv − mu) / t**, force = change in momentum ÷ time.
Work done = force × distance and KE = ½ × m × v² can also give the average force over a stopping distance.
A deceleration gives a negative value of a; the size of the force is what matters in estimates.

callouts.p: A negative acceleration: the rate of decrease of velocity, measured in m/s².

core.p: Estimate questions give little data, so you must supply sensible values. Use round numbers and give your answer to one or two significant figures.
bullets: Mass of a car: about **1000 kg to 1500 kg**; a person: about **70 kg**; a lorry: about **10 000 kg to 40 000 kg**.
Speed in town (30 mph): about **13 m/s**; motorway (70 mph): about **30 m/s**.
Walking: about 1.5 m/s; cycling: about 6 m/s.
Normal braking to rest from 13 m/s takes a few seconds: deceleration of a few m/s².
A crash with a solid object stops a car in roughly **0.1 s**, or over the length of the crumple zone (about 0.5 m).
g = 10 m/s²: decelerations are sometimes compared with g (e.g. 50 m/s² is 5g).

callouts.p: Write down the values you assume (e.g. 'mass of car ≈ 1000 kg'). Marks are given for sensible values and correct use of the equation, not for one exact answer.

core.h: Estimating the force in a crash
core.p: A car of mass about 1000 kg travelling at about 13 m/s (30 mph) hits a wall and stops in about 0.1 s.
bullets: Deceleration a = (v − u) / t = (0 − 13) / 0.1 = −130 m/s², so about 130 m/s².
For a 70 kg passenger: F = 70 × 130 ≈ 9000 N, about 13 times their weight (700 N).
If the stopping time were 1 s instead, the force would be 10 times smaller.
Compare with emergency braking: about 1000 × 7 = 7000 N.

callouts.p: Forces in road crashes are typically tens or hundreds of thousands of newtons on a car, and thousands of newtons on a person.

core.p: If you know (or estimate) the distance over which something stops, use v² − u² = 2ax to find the deceleration, then F = m × a.
bullets: Car at 20 m/s crumples 0.5 m: a = (0 − 20²) / (2 × 0.5) = −400 m/s², size 400 m/s².
For a 70 kg person held by a seat belt that also stretches, the stopping distance might be about 0.7 m in total, reducing the deceleration.
Doubling the stopping distance **halves** the deceleration and so halves the force.
Doubling the speed with the same stopping distance makes the deceleration **four times** larger, because a depends on v².

callouts.p: In v² − u² = 2ax remember to square the speed: 20² = 400, not 40.

core.h: Force and rate of change of momentum (Higher)
core.p: Momentum p = m × v. Newton's second law can be written as force = change in momentum ÷ time taken. In a crash the change in momentum is fixed (from mv to zero), so the only way to reduce the force is to make the time longer.
bullets: Same change in momentum, longer time → smaller force.
This is the physics behind crumple zones, seat belts, air bags, helmets and crash mats.
On a force-time graph the area under the graph equals the change in momentum; spreading the impact over a longer time gives a lower, wider curve with the same area.

callouts.t: Force as rate of change of momentum
callouts.p: The resultant force on an object equals the rate of change of its momentum: F = (mv − mu) / t.

core.p: The front and rear of a car are designed to crumple (squash) in a controlled way in a collision, while the passenger cell stays rigid.
bullets: Crumpling **increases the time** taken for the car to stop.
This **reduces the deceleration** and so the **force** on the occupants.
Work is done deforming the metal, which transfers energy away from the kinetic store of the car.
The rigid passenger cell protects people from being crushed.

core.p: Without restraint, a passenger keeps moving forward (inertia) until they hit the dashboard or windscreen, stopping in a very short time. Restraints make them stop with the car over a longer time.
bullets: **Seat belts** stretch slightly, increasing the time for the passenger to stop and spreading the force across the chest and pelvis (stronger parts of the body).
Seat belts also stop the passenger hitting the inside of the car or being thrown out.
**Air bags** inflate in a fraction of a second and then deflate as the person hits them, increasing the stopping time and spreading the force over a larger area.
Seat belts must be replaced after a crash because they have been stretched.
Head restraints reduce whiplash by limiting the backward movement of the head.

callouts.p: Seat belts and air bags do NOT reduce the change in momentum; they increase the TIME, which reduces the deceleration and force.

core.h: Other safety features on the road
core.p: The same idea, increase the stopping time or distance, appears in many other road-safety features.
bullets: **Cycle and motorcycle helmets**: a crushable foam layer increases the time for the head to stop.
**Crash barriers** on motorways bend and absorb energy, stopping cars over a longer time.
**Gravel traps** and **run-off areas** let a vehicle stop over a longer distance.
**Collapsible steering columns** reduce chest injuries.
**Child car seats** hold small children securely.
**ABS (anti-lock brakes)** stop wheels locking during hard braking, so the driver keeps control.
