core.p: Being able to explain what increases the danger is as important as the calculations.
bullets: **Higher speed**: larger change in velocity to remove, so larger deceleration for the same time.
**Shorter stopping time** or **shorter stopping distance** (hitting a rigid object such as a wall or tree).
**No seat belt**: the body stops suddenly against a hard surface.
**Heavier vehicles** (Higher: more momentum) hitting lighter ones: the lighter vehicle has a larger change in velocity.
Pedestrians and cyclists have no crumple zone, so lower speed limits in towns reduce their injuries.

core.p: Six-mark questions often ask you to explain how a safety feature reduces injury, or to compare two situations using estimates.
bullets: Start with the physics idea: force depends on deceleration (F = m × a) or on rate of change of momentum.
Say what the feature changes: it increases the **time** (or distance) of the collision.
Then the effect: smaller deceleration, so smaller force on the person.
Finish with the outcome: less chance of serious injury.
Use numbers if given: a calculated force before and after strengthens the answer.

callouts.p: Mark schemes look for: increases time, reduces deceleration (or rate of change of momentum), reduces force.

analogy.p: If you catch a thrown egg with stiff hands it stops in an instant and breaks: a huge deceleration and a huge force. If you move your hands back as you catch it, the egg stops over a longer time and distance, so the deceleration and force are small and it survives. Crumple zones, seat belts and air bags are the car's 'soft hands'. Where it breaks down: a car crash involves the car, its occupants and the object hit all deforming, and the energy goes into bending metal and heating rather than just into your hands, but the physics of a longer stopping time giving a smaller force is the same.

terms.d: Negative acceleration; the rate at which velocity decreases, in m/s².
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object; F = m × a.
The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass: F = m × a.
Mass × velocity, p = m × v, measured in kg m/s (Higher).
Change in momentum divided by time taken, equal to the resultant force (Higher).
The tendency of an object to stay at rest or keep moving at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts.
Part of a vehicle designed to deform in a collision, increasing the stopping time and reducing the force on occupants.
A restraint that stretches slightly, increasing the time for the occupant to stop and spreading the force.
A bag that inflates in a crash, increasing the stopping time of the head and chest and spreading the force over a larger area.
An approximate value worked out using sensible assumed values, usually to one or two significant figures.
The power of ten closest to a value, e.g. 130 000 N is of order 10⁵ N.
A neck injury caused when the head is jerked forwards and backwards by a sudden large deceleration.
Sliding of locked wheels over the road when braking force needed is larger than friction available.
The time over which a collision force acts; increasing it reduces the force for the same change in momentum.

mistakes.w: Crumple zones absorb the force.
mistakes.r: Crumple zones increase the time of the collision, reducing the deceleration and so the force on the occupants.

mistakes.w: Seat belts reduce the momentum of the passenger.
mistakes.r: The change in momentum is the same; seat belts increase the time taken for it to change, so the force is smaller.

mistakes.w: Air bags make the person stop more quickly.
mistakes.r: Air bags increase the time taken to stop, reducing deceleration and force.

mistakes.w: Uses 30 m/s for a car in town or 1 kg for a car's mass.
mistakes.r: Use sensible values: about 13 m/s in town, about 1000 kg for a car.

mistakes.w: Writes v² − u² = 2ax as 20 × 2 = 2 × a × 0.5.
mistakes.r: Square the speed: 20² = 400, so a = 400 / (2 × 0.5) = 400 m/s².

mistakes.w: A larger force is needed because the car has more speed (F = m × v).
mistakes.r: Force depends on deceleration (F = m × a) or rate of change of momentum, not on speed alone.

mistakes.w: Gives the deceleration as the answer when asked for force.
mistakes.r: Multiply the deceleration by the mass: F = m × a, unit N.

mistakes.w: Large decelerations are dangerous because the car goes fast.
mistakes.r: Large decelerations need large forces (F = m × a), and large forces on the body cause injury.

exam.q: State the equation linking force, mass and acceleration.
model: force = mass × acceleration (F = m × a).
exam.tip: Learn the word equation as well as the symbols.

exam.q: Explain why large decelerations are dangerous for people in a car.
model: Large deceleration requires a large force (F = m × a).
Large forces on the body cause injury.
exam.tip: Link deceleration to force.

exam.q: Estimate the mass of a family car.
model: Any value 800 kg to 2000 kg (e.g. 1000 kg).
exam.tip: Give units.

exam.q: A car travelling at 15 m/s hits a wall and stops in 0.10 s. Calculate the deceleration.
model: = −150 m/s² (deceleration of 150 m/s²).
exam.tip: Either sign is accepted if you call it a deceleration.

exam.q: The car in the previous question has a mass of 1200 kg. Calculate the force on the car.
exam.tip: Carry forward your deceleration from the previous part.

exam.q: Explain how a crumple zone reduces injury in a collision.
model: Crumple zone increases the time taken for the car to stop.
So the deceleration is smaller / rate of change of momentum is smaller.
So the force on the occupants is smaller (less injury).
exam.tip: Three-step chain: time, deceleration, force.

exam.q: A cyclist of mass 70 kg (including bike) travelling at 6 m/s stops in 3 s. Estimate the braking force.
exam.tip: Answer is a magnitude.

exam.q: (Higher) A 70 kg passenger moving at 13 m/s is brought to rest by a seat belt in 0.2 s. Calculate the force on the passenger.
model: Change in momentum = 70 × 13 − 0 = 910 kg m/s.
F = change in momentum / time = 910 / 0.2
exam.tip: Use F = (mv − mu) / t.

exam.q: Estimate the deceleration of a car travelling at 30 m/s that crumples 0.75 m when it hits a barrier.
model: = −600 m/s² (deceleration 600 m/s²).
exam.tip: Square the speed first.

exam.q: Explain how seat belts, air bags and crumple zones work together to reduce injuries in a car crash. Use ideas about forces in your answer.
model: In a crash the car and occupants have a large change in velocity/momentum.
Force = mass × deceleration (or rate of change of momentum), so a short stopping time means a large force.
Crumple zones deform, increasing the time for the car to stop.
Seat belts stretch, increasing the time for the occupant to stop and keeping them from hitting the car's interior.
Air bags increase the stopping time of the head/chest and spread the force over a larger area.
Longer time gives smaller deceleration so smaller force on the body, so fewer/less serious injuries.
exam.tip: Cover all three features and finish with the force consequence.

worked.q: Estimate the force on a car hitting a tree at 30 mph. Assume a mass of 1000 kg, a speed of 13 m/s and a stopping time of 0.1 s.
steps: Round for an estimate: about 1 × 10⁵ N.

worked.q: A 70 kg driver travelling at 20 m/s is stopped by an air bag over 0.40 m. Without it, her head would stop over 0.05 m against the steering wheel. Compare the forces.
worked.ans: The air bag reduces the force by a factor of 8 (35 000 N compared with 280 000 N), because the stopping distance is 8 times longer.

worked.q: (Higher) A 1500 kg car moving at 20 m/s stops in a crash. With crumple zones the collision lasts 0.25 s; without them 0.05 s. Find the force in each case.
worked.ans: 120 000 N with crumple zones and 600 000 N without: 5 times longer time gives 5 times smaller force.

phy_edx.1.16.summary: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance, and both grow with speed, but not in the same way. Thinking distance is proportional to speed (distance = speed × reaction time), while braking distance is proportional to the **square of the initial speed**, because the work done by the brakes (F × d) must equal the car's kinetic energy (½mv²). This triple-only point asks you to estimate emergency stopping distances over typical road speeds (about 12 m at 20 mph up to about 96 m at 70 mph) and to use work done = change in kinetic energy to show why doubling speed makes braking distance four times longer.

core.h: 1. What stopping distance is made of
core.p: When a driver sees a hazard, the car keeps moving at full speed while the driver reacts, and only then starts to slow down. So the total stopping distance has two parts that simply add together.
bullets: **Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance**
**Thinking distance**: distance travelled during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied; the car is still at its original speed
**Braking distance**: distance travelled from when the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops
Thinking distance = speed × reaction time (constant speed, so distance = speed × time)
Braking distance depends on the speed, the mass of the vehicle and the size of the braking force (which depends on brakes, tyres and road surface)
This point (2.32P-2.33P) is about how both parts change across typical road speeds

callouts.p: The total distance travelled from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment the vehicle stops: thinking distance + braking distance.

Tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions affect thinking distance (reaction time). Wet or icy roads, worn tyres and worn brakes affect braking distance. Speed and mass affect braking distance; speed also affects thinking distance.

core.p: The Highway Code gives typical stopping distances for a car in good conditions. You are expected to estimate how stopping distance varies over this range of typical speeds and to recognise the pattern.
bullets: Speeds on UK roads range from about 20 mph (about 9 m/s) in towns up to 70 mph (about 31 m/s) on motorways
At 20 mph the total is about **12 m** (roughly 3 car lengths)
At 70 mph the total is about **96 m** (roughly 24 car lengths)
The speed has increased 3.5 times but the stopping distance has increased about 8 times
At low speed the two parts are similar; at high speed **braking distance dominates**
Useful conversion: 1 mph ≈ 0.45 m/s, so 30 mph ≈ 13 m/s and 70 mph ≈ 31 m/s

callouts.p: A good estimate for a car at 30 mph is about 23 m to stop, and at 70 mph about 96 m. These are for a dry road and an alert driver; real distances are often longer.

core.h: 3. Thinking distance is proportional to speed
core.p: During the reaction time the car is not slowing down at all, so it travels at constant speed. Distance = speed × time, and if the reaction time stays the same, the thinking distance is directly proportional to speed.
bullets: **Thinking distance = speed × reaction time**
Typical reaction time is about 0.7 s for an alert driver (it can range from about 0.2 s to 0.9 s; much longer if tired, drunk or distracted)
Double the speed → double the thinking distance (if reaction time is unchanged)
In the table: 6 m, 9 m, 12 m, 15 m, 18 m, 21 m goes up by 3 m for every 10 mph: a straight-line pattern
A thinking distance against speed graph is a **straight line through the origin**
Example: 20 m/s × 0.7 s = 14 m

callouts.p: If a question gives a table and asks you to describe the thinking distance pattern, say it is directly proportional to speed and quote a pair of values that show doubling (for example 20 mph to 40 mph: 6 m to 12 m).

core.h: 4. Braking distance is proportional to speed squared
core.p: Braking distance does not rise in a straight line. The data show that doubling the speed makes the braking distance about four times larger: 20 mph gives 6 m but 40 mph gives 24 m. This is because braking distance ∝ v².
bullets: **Braking distance ∝ (initial speed)²** for the same braking force and mass
Double the speed → braking distance × 4 (2²)
Triple the speed → braking distance × 9 (3²)
Check from the table: 20 mph → 6 m, 60 mph → 55 m, roughly 9 times (3² = 9)
A braking distance against speed graph is a **curve getting steeper** (half a parabola), not a straight line
A graph of braking distance against speed² is a straight line through the origin

callouts.p: Because of the v² relationship, a small increase in speed causes a large increase in braking distance. Going from 30 mph to 40 mph increases braking distance from 14 m to 24 m: a 33% rise in speed gives about a 70% rise in braking distance.

core.h: 5. Work done by the brakes equals the kinetic energy
core.p: To stop the car, the brakes must remove all of its kinetic energy. The braking force does work on the car, and work done = force × distance. So the work done by the brakes over the braking distance must equal the car's initial kinetic energy.
bullets: **Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force**: W = F × d
**Kinetic energy = ½ × mass × (speed)²**: KE = ½ × m × v²
To bring the car to rest: **work done by brakes = initial kinetic energy**
So **F × d = ½ × m × v²**
Rearranged: **d = (m × v²) ÷ (2 × F)**
With F and m fixed, d is proportional to v², which proves the pattern in the data
Units: F in newtons (N), d in metres (m), m in kilograms (kg), v in metres per second (m/s), energy and work in joules (J)

callouts.p: Work done to stop = F × d. Kinetic energy = ½mv². These are equal, so d = mv² ÷ 2F. For a given car and braking force, braking distance ∝ v².
Speeds in mph or km/h must be converted to m/s before using ½mv², or the energy and distance will be wrong.

core.h: 6. Why v² and not v: the reasoning
core.p: Kinetic energy depends on v², so a car going twice as fast has four times as much kinetic energy to get rid of. The brakes can only supply roughly the same maximum force, so the only way to do four times the work is to act over four times the distance.
bullets: KE ∝ v²: at 2v, KE = ½m(2v)² = 4 × ½mv²
Maximum braking force is limited by the grip (friction) between tyres and road, so F does not increase with speed
Same F, four times the work needed → four times the distance
This is why speed limits near schools are low: a small reduction in speed cuts braking distance a lot
Mass also matters: d ∝ m for the same force, so a fully loaded van needs a longer braking distance than an empty one

callouts.p: Only braking distance is proportional to v². Total stopping distance includes thinking distance (∝ v), so doubling speed makes the total more than double but less than four times.

fig.cap: Doubling the speed doubles the thinking distance but makes the braking distance four times as long, because braking distance depends on speed squared. The numbers are in units of the thinking or braking distance at speed v.

core.p: Exam calculations usually give the mass, the initial speed and the braking force. Find the kinetic energy first, then divide by the braking force to get the distance.
bullets: Step 1: convert speed to m/s if needed
Step 2: KE = ½ × m × v²
Step 3: work done by brakes = KE
Step 4: d = work done ÷ F
Alternatively find F if d is given: F = KE ÷ d
Always give the unit (m for distance, N for force, J for energy)

callouts.p: In ½mv², only v is squared. Work out v² first, then multiply by m, then halve. A common error is (½ × m × v)².

core.p: The same result appears from the equation of motion. If a car decelerates uniformly from speed u to rest, v = 0, so 0 - u² = 2ax, giving braking distance x = u² ÷ 2a (using the size of the deceleration). For a fixed deceleration, braking distance is again proportional to u².
bullets: **Braking distance x = u² ÷ (2 × deceleration)**
Deceleration a = F ÷ m (Newton's second law), so x = u²m ÷ 2F: exactly the energy result
Typical car braking deceleration on a dry road is about 6 to 8 m/s²
On an icy road the maximum deceleration may be only about 1 to 2 m/s², so braking distance can be several times longer
Both methods (energy and equations of motion) give the same answer: use whichever the question data suit

callouts.p: Energy route: F × d = ½mv². Motion route: v² - u² = 2ax with a = F/m. They are the same physics.

core.h: 9. Estimating stopping distance at any typical speed
core.p: To estimate an emergency stopping distance you need sensible values for reaction time and deceleration, then add the two parts. Estimation questions reward reasonable assumptions and clear working, not exact answers.
bullets: Thinking distance ≈ speed × 0.7 s
Braking distance ≈ speed² ÷ (2 × 7 m/s²) for a dry road
Example at 13 m/s (30 mph): thinking ≈ 9 m, braking ≈ 169 ÷ 14 ≈ 12 m, total ≈ 21 m (Highway Code: 23 m)
Example at 31 m/s (70 mph): thinking ≈ 22 m, braking ≈ 961 ÷ 14 ≈ 69 m, total ≈ 91 m (Highway Code: 96 m)
State your assumptions: alert driver, dry road, good tyres and brakes
Round to 1 or 2 significant figures for an estimate

callouts.p: Write 'assume reaction time 0.7 s' or 'assume deceleration 7 m/s²' in your working. Examiners give credit for a sensible stated value.

core.h: 10. Conditions that change the braking distance
core.p: The v² rule assumes the braking force stays the same. Anything that reduces the maximum braking force, or increases the mass, makes the braking distance longer at every speed, and the effect is much bigger at high speed.
bullets: **Wet or icy road**: less friction between tyres and road, so smaller maximum braking force → longer braking distance
**Worn tyres** (less tread): less grip, especially in the wet
**Worn brakes**: smaller braking force
**Greater mass** (passengers, luggage, a loaded lorry): more kinetic energy at the same speed → longer braking distance
**Higher speed**: more kinetic energy, braking distance ∝ v²
If the braking force is halved (for example on a slippery road) the braking distance doubles at every speed

core.p: When a car brakes, work done by the friction force between brake pads and discs transfers energy from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes, which then dissipates to the surroundings.
bullets: Kinetic energy store of car → thermal energy store of brakes (and tyres, road, air)
Brakes can become very hot during hard or repeated braking
Overheated brakes become less effective (brake fade), increasing braking distance
Energy is conserved: all of the ½mv² ends up as thermal energy (and a little sound)

callouts.p: Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance: work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.

core.p: The v² relationship explains much of road safety design. Because braking distance grows so quickly with speed, the gap a driver needs to leave grows much faster than the speed itself.
bullets: Drivers must leave a bigger gap at higher speed (the two-second rule helps)
On wet roads the gap should be at least doubled; on ice it may need to be ten times bigger
Low speed limits in towns (20 or 30 mph) keep stopping distances short where pedestrians are present
At higher speed the car still has more kinetic energy when it hits something it could not avoid, so the impact is more dangerous
Interpreting data: questions may ask you to read stopping distances off a chart and comment on safety

callouts.p: Charts may give speeds in mph or km/h. Only convert to m/s when you need to calculate energy or use equations of motion.

analogy.p: Think of the car's kinetic energy as a debt the brakes must pay off, and the braking force as a fixed payment per metre travelled. Doubling the speed does not double the debt; it multiplies it by four, because KE = ½mv². With the same payment per metre, you need four times as many metres to clear it. Thinking distance is different: it is like a meter that runs at a steady rate while you hesitate, so it only doubles. Where it breaks down: a real debt can be paid faster by paying more, but the braking force has a maximum set by tyre grip, and on ice the 'payment per metre' falls sharply, which is why the analogy needs the force to be treated as limited.

terms.d: Total distance travelled from seeing a hazard to the vehicle stopping; thinking distance + braking distance.
Distance travelled during the driver's reaction time, at the original speed, before the brakes are applied.
Distance travelled from when the brakes are applied until the vehicle comes to rest.
Time between the driver seeing a hazard and applying the brakes; typically about 0.7 s for an alert driver.
Energy in the kinetic store of a moving object; KE = ½ × m × v², measured in joules.
Energy transferred when a force moves through a distance; work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.
The friction force that opposes the vehicle's motion when the brakes are applied, measured in newtons.
Rate of decrease of velocity, in m/s²; a = F ÷ m.
Two quantities are directly proportional if doubling one doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
If one quantity is ∝ v², doubling v multiplies it by 4 and tripling v multiplies it by 9.
A force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact, such as brake pads and discs, or tyres and road.
The store that increases when objects warm up; braking transfers kinetic energy to the thermal store of the brakes.
A calculation using sensible approximate values to get an answer of the right size, usually to 1 or 2 significant figures.
A realistic speed for a situation, for example about 13 m/s (30 mph) in a town or 31 m/s (70 mph) on a motorway.

mistakes.w: Doubling the speed doubles the braking distance.
mistakes.r: Braking distance ∝ v², so doubling speed makes braking distance four times longer.

mistakes.w: Doubling the speed makes the stopping distance four times longer.
mistakes.r: Only the braking distance quadruples; thinking distance only doubles, so total stopping distance increases by between two and four times.

mistakes.w: Being tired increases the braking distance.
mistakes.r: Tiredness increases reaction time, so it increases the thinking distance; braking distance is unchanged.

mistakes.w: Using speed in mph or km/h in KE = ½mv².
mistakes.r: Convert speed to m/s first so that KE comes out in joules.

mistakes.w: KE = ½ × m × v, or squaring the whole of ½mv.
mistakes.r: KE = ½ × m × v²: only the speed is squared.

mistakes.w: Braking distance = speed × braking time, using the initial speed.
mistakes.r: Speed is not constant during braking; use F × d = ½mv² or v² - u² = 2ax.

mistakes.w: The kinetic energy is destroyed when the car stops.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes and surroundings by work done by the friction force; it is not destroyed.

mistakes.w: Wet roads increase the thinking distance.
mistakes.r: Wet roads reduce friction between tyres and road, reducing the braking force and increasing the braking distance.

mistakes.w: Braking distance against speed is a straight line.
mistakes.r: It is a curve getting steeper; braking distance against speed squared is a straight line through the origin.

exam.q: State what is meant by the stopping distance of a car.
model: Thinking distance + braking distance (total distance from seeing hazard to stopping)
exam.tip: Naming both parts added together is enough for the mark.

exam.q: A car travelling at 20 mph has a braking distance of 6 m. Estimate its braking distance at 40 mph, assuming the same braking force.
model: Speed doubles, braking distance ∝ v², so × 4
Braking distance = 24 m
exam.tip: Spot the scale factor for speed, then square it.

exam.q: Explain why the braking distance of a car increases with the square of its initial speed.
model: Kinetic energy = ½mv², so KE ∝ v²
To stop, all KE must be transferred by work done by the brakes
Work done = braking force × braking distance
For the same braking force, braking distance ∝ KE, so ∝ v²
exam.tip: Link KE, work done and distance in a chain; quote both equations.

exam.q: A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at 15 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy of the car.
exam.tip: Square the speed first: 15² = 225.

exam.q: The car in the previous question brakes with a constant braking force of 5400 N. Calculate the braking distance.
model: Work done = KE = 135 000 J
d = work done ÷ F = 135 000 ÷ 5400
d = 25 m
exam.tip: Say that work done by the brakes equals the KE before dividing.

exam.q: A car travels at 31 m/s. Estimate the thinking distance for an alert driver.
model: Use reaction time ≈ 0.7 s (accept 0.5 to 0.9 s)
Thinking distance = 31 × 0.7 ≈ 22 m
exam.tip: State your reaction time value clearly.

exam.q: Describe how the thinking distance and braking distance change as speed increases from 20 mph to 70 mph.
model: Thinking distance increases in proportion to speed
e.g. 6 m at 20 mph to 21 m at 70 mph
Braking distance increases more rapidly / ∝ speed²
e.g. 6 m at 20 mph to 75 m at 70 mph; braking distance becomes the larger part
exam.tip: Use data from the table to support each statement.

exam.q: A loaded lorry has twice the mass of the empty lorry. Explain the effect on its braking distance at the same speed and braking force.
model: KE doubles because KE ∝ m
Same braking force, so braking distance doubles
exam.tip: Mass is not squared.

exam.q: Explain why the braking distance on an icy road is greater than on a dry road for the same speed.
model: Less friction between tyres and road
So the maximum braking force is smaller
Same KE must be transferred, so a greater distance is needed (d = KE ÷ F)
exam.tip: Tie the friction to the force and then to work done.

exam.q: A student says 'If I drive twice as fast I need twice as much room to stop.' Using ideas about thinking distance, braking distance and energy, evaluate this statement.
model: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
Thinking distance = speed × reaction time, so it doubles when speed doubles
KE = ½mv², so doubling speed makes KE four times greater
Work done by brakes = F × d must equal KE
For the same braking force, braking distance becomes four times greater
So total stopping distance more than doubles; the student is wrong (it is between 2 and 4 times)
exam.tip: In a 6 mark answer, deal with both parts of stopping distance and finish with a clear judgement.

exam.q: A car of mass 900 kg travelling at 20 m/s stops in a braking distance of 30 m. Calculate the average braking force.
exam.tip: Rearrange F × d = ½mv² for F.

worked.q: A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at 20 m/s. The brakes provide a constant force of 6000 N. Calculate the braking distance. Then calculate the braking distance at 30 m/s and show it agrees with braking distance ∝ v².
steps: Work done by brakes = KE, so F × d = 240 000 J
worked.ans: 40 m at 20 m/s and 90 m at 30 m/s; distance has increased by 1.5² = 2.25 times, confirming braking distance ∝ v².

worked.q: Estimate the emergency stopping distance of a car travelling at 30 m/s on a dry road. Assume a reaction time of 0.7 s and a braking deceleration of 7 m/s².
steps: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time = 30 × 0.7 = 21 m
Braking distance: v² - u² = 2ax with v = 0, so x = u² ÷ 2a
worked.ans: About 85 m (roughly 90 m to 1 s.f.), with braking distance making up about three quarters of the total.

worked.q: A car has a thinking distance of 9 m and a braking distance of 14 m at 30 mph. Estimate its stopping distance at 60 mph for the same driver and road.
worked.ans: About 74 m (the Highway Code value is 73 m), more than three times the stopping distance at 30 mph.

phy_edx.1.7.summary: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and stays the same wherever the object is, but weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass, so it changes with the gravitational field strength. The two are linked by the equation weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = m x g), with g about 10 N/kg on Earth. Weight is a force, so it is a vector measured in newtons using a newton meter (a calibrated spring balance), and it is directly proportional to both mass and gravitational field strength.

core.p: **Mass** measures how much matter (stuff) an object contains. It is measured in **kilograms (kg)**. Because the number and type of particles in an object do not change when you move it, its mass is the same on Earth, on the Moon or floating in deep space.
bullets: Mass is a **scalar** quantity: it has size (magnitude) only, no direction.
Unit: kilogram (kg). Convert grams to kg by dividing by 1000 before using any equation.
Mass only changes if matter is added or removed, for example a rocket burning fuel loses mass.
Mass is measured with a **top-pan balance** (which is calibrated to read in grams or kilograms).
Mass also tells you how hard an object is to accelerate (its inertia), which links to Newton's second law.

callouts.p: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg). It does not depend on location.

core.p: **Weight** is the **force acting on an object due to gravity**. Any object with mass is pulled towards other masses such as the Earth. Because weight is a force it is measured in **newtons (N)**, and it always acts towards the centre of the planet or moon (downwards for us).
bullets: Weight is a **vector**: it has magnitude and direction (towards the centre of the Earth).
Unit: newton (N), the same unit as every other force.
Weight is a **non-contact force**: the Earth does not need to touch the object to pull it.
On a free body diagram weight is drawn as an arrow starting from the **centre of mass** pointing straight down.
Weight changes if the gravitational field strength changes, even though mass does not.

callouts.p: The force acting on an object due to gravity (the gravitational force of the Earth on the object), measured in newtons (N).

core.p: A **gravitational field** is the region around a mass where another mass feels a force. The **gravitational field strength (g)** tells you how many newtons of force act on each kilogram of mass, so its unit is **newtons per kilogram (N/kg)**.
bullets: On Earth g is about **10 N/kg** (more precisely about 9.8 N/kg). Edexcel questions normally tell you to use 10 N/kg.
On the Moon g is about **1.6 N/kg**, roughly one sixth of Earth's value.
g depends on the **mass of the planet** (more mass, stronger field) and on **how far you are from its centre** (further away, weaker field).
Near the Earth's surface g is effectively constant, so weight is the same at ground level everywhere you are likely to test it.
g in N/kg is numerically equal to the acceleration of free fall in m/s² (10 m/s² on Earth).

head: Place
g (N/kg)
Weight of a 60 kg person (N)
rows: Deep space, far from any mass

callouts.p: N/kg and m/s² are equivalent units: 1 N/kg = 1 m/s². Use N/kg when talking about weight.

core.h: The equation W = m x g
core.p: You must **recall and use** this equation: **weight (N) = mass (kg) x gravitational field strength (N/kg)**, or W = m x g. It works because g is the force on each kilogram, so multiplying by the number of kilograms gives the total force.
bullets: W = m x g, so m = W / g and g = W / m.
Always put mass in **kg**: 500 g = 0.5 kg.
Weight answers must be in **N**; mass answers in **kg**; g answers in **N/kg**.
Show your working: write the equation, substitute, then give the answer with unit.
This is a special case of F = m x a, where the force is weight and the acceleration is g.

callouts.p: Cover the quantity you want: W on top, m and g underneath. Covering m leaves W / g.

core.h: Weight is directly proportional to mass
core.p: Because W = m x g and g is constant in one place, **weight is directly proportional to mass**. Double the mass and the weight doubles. A graph of weight (y-axis) against mass (x-axis) is a **straight line through the origin**.
bullets: Gradient of the weight-mass graph = W / m = **g**.
A steeper line means a stronger gravitational field (for example Earth compared with the Moon).
The line passes through the origin because zero mass has zero weight.
Weight is also directly proportional to g for a fixed mass: double g and the weight doubles.
Writing W ∝ m shows the proportional relationship.

callouts.p: Straight line through the origin = directly proportional. Say both parts in an exam answer.

core.h: Measuring weight with a newton meter
core.p: Weight is measured using a **calibrated spring balance**, called a **newton meter** (forcemeter). Hang the object from the hook: gravity pulls it down, the spring stretches, and the stretch is shown on a scale marked in newtons.
bullets: It works because the **extension of the spring is proportional to the force** (Hooke's law), so the scale is evenly spaced.
Hold the newton meter **vertically** and wait for the object to stop moving before reading.
Check the meter reads **zero** with nothing on it (avoid a zero error); adjust it if not.
Choose a meter with a suitable range: too small a range and the spring overstretches; too large and the reading is not precise.
Read the scale at eye level to avoid parallax error.
A top-pan balance actually detects the force on its pan but is calibrated in grams/kg using g on Earth, so it would give the wrong mass on the Moon.

callouts.p: A calibrated spring balance used to measure force (including weight) in newtons.

core.p: Students lose marks by mixing up mass and weight. In everyday speech people say 'I weigh 60 kilograms', but in physics 60 kg is a **mass**; the weight is 600 N.
bullets: Mass is fixed; weight depends on where you are.
Mass is scalar; weight is vector.
Mass in kg; weight in N.
Mass measured with a balance; weight measured with a newton meter.
An astronaut in orbit still has the same mass and is still pulled by gravity (g is only slightly smaller at the height of the ISS); they feel weightless because they are in free fall.

callouts.t: kg is never a unit of weight
callouts.p: If the question asks for weight, the unit must be N. Writing kg loses the unit mark.

core.h: Weight on other planets and moons
core.p: Taking an object to the Moon does not change its mass, but the Moon has much less mass than the Earth, so its gravitational field strength is smaller and the object's weight is smaller.
bullets: Weight on the Moon = mass x 1.6 N/kg, about one sixth of the weight on Earth.
A larger planet does not automatically have a larger g: g depends on mass and radius together, so use the value given.
To compare, first find the mass (it is the same everywhere), then multiply by the new g.
Lower weight on the Moon is why astronauts can jump higher and carry heavy backpacks, even though the backpack is just as hard to start moving (same mass).

callouts.p: Given a weight on Earth and asked for weight on the Moon: m = W / 10, then W(Moon) = m x 1.6.

core.h: Weight acts from the centre of mass
core.p: Although gravity pulls on every particle in an object, we can treat the whole weight as acting at a single point called the **centre of mass**. This makes free body diagrams simpler.
bullets: For a regular shape of even density, the centre of mass is at its geometric centre.
Draw the weight arrow from the centre of mass, pointing vertically downwards.
The length of the arrow represents the size of the force.
If an object rests on a surface, the normal contact force (reaction) acts upwards and balances the weight when it is stationary.

core.p: When weight is the only force acting (free fall with no air resistance), the resultant force is the weight. Using F = m x a, m x g = m x a, so **a = g**. That is why all objects fall with the same acceleration (about 10 m/s²) in a vacuum.
bullets: A heavier object has a bigger weight but also a bigger mass to accelerate; the two cancel, so the acceleration is the same.
In air, air resistance increases with speed until it equals the weight; then the resultant force is zero and the object reaches terminal velocity.
Weight is the force that provides the accelerating force for a falling object or a hanging mass pulling a trolley.

callouts.p: g is both the force per kilogram (N/kg) and the free-fall acceleration (m/s²).

core.p: Exam calculations often need rearranging or a unit conversion. Being systematic earns full marks even if you make a slip at the end.
bullets: Grams to kilograms: divide by 1000 (250 g = 0.25 kg).
Kilonewtons to newtons: multiply by 1000 (2.5 kN = 2500 N).
Tonnes to kilograms: multiply by 1000 (1.2 tonnes = 1200 kg).
To find mass from a newton meter reading: m = W / g.
Give answers to a sensible number of significant figures, matching the data.

callouts.p: Using 250 instead of 0.25 in W = m x g gives an answer 1000 times too big.

analogy.t: Bag of sugar and a pulling hand
analogy.p: Think of mass as the number of sugar bags in a box: it is the same wherever you carry the box. Gravitational field strength is how hard an invisible hand pulls on each bag (10 N per kg on Earth, 1.6 N per kg on the Moon). Weight is the total pull, the number of bags times the pull per bag. Where it breaks down: a real hand only pulls on what it touches, but gravity is a non-contact force that acts on every particle at once, and the 'hand' is really the attraction between the object's mass and the planet's mass, so the object pulls back on the planet with an equal force too.

terms.d: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg); it does not change with location.
The force acting on an object due to gravity, measured in newtons (N).
The force of gravity acting on each kilogram of mass, measured in N/kg; about 10 N/kg on Earth.
The region around a mass in which another mass experiences a force.
The unit of force; 1 N gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
A calibrated spring balance used to measure force, including weight, in newtons.
Marked with a scale checked against known values so that readings are accurate.
An instrument used to measure mass, reading in grams or kilograms.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass.
A quantity with magnitude and direction, such as weight.
Two quantities that increase in the same ratio; their graph is a straight line through the origin.
The single point at which the weight of an object can be considered to act.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, such as gravitational force.
When an instrument does not read zero when nothing is being measured, making every reading wrong by the same amount.

mistakes.w: My weight is 55 kg.
mistakes.r: 55 kg is a mass. Weight = 55 x 10 = 550 N.

mistakes.w: On the Moon your mass is less because gravity is weaker.
mistakes.r: Mass stays the same; weight is less because gravitational field strength is smaller.

mistakes.w: Weight and mass are the same thing.
mistakes.r: Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the force due to gravity on that mass (N).

mistakes.w: W = m x g with m = 400 (grams).
mistakes.r: Convert to kg first: m = 0.4 kg, W = 0.4 x 10 = 4 N.

mistakes.w: Weight is measured with a top-pan balance.
mistakes.r: Weight is measured with a newton meter (calibrated spring balance).

mistakes.w: Astronauts in orbit have no weight because there is no gravity in space.
mistakes.r: Gravity still acts on them (g is only slightly lower); they feel weightless because they are in free fall.

mistakes.w: g = 10 kg/N
mistakes.r: The unit of gravitational field strength is N/kg (newtons per kilogram).

mistakes.w: Weight is proportional to mass because the line goes up.
mistakes.r: It is directly proportional because the graph is a straight line through the origin.

exam.q: State the unit of gravitational field strength.
model: N/kg (newtons per kilogram); accept m/s²
exam.tip: Write the unit in full or with the correct symbols; kg/N scores zero.

exam.q: Write down the equation that links weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
model: weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = m x g)
exam.tip: Words or standard symbols both score; do not invent your own letters.

exam.q: A bag of potatoes has a mass of 2.5 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: W = 25 N
exam.tip: Give the unit N; the answer mark often needs it.

exam.q: An astronaut has a weight of 800 N on Earth. Calculate the astronaut's weight on the Moon, where g = 1.6 N/kg. (Earth g = 10 N/kg)
model: m = 80 kg
exam.tip: Find the mass first; it is the same on Earth and on the Moon.

exam.q: Explain the difference between mass and weight.
model: Mass is the amount of matter in an object (measured in kg) and does not change with location
Weight is the force due to gravity acting on the mass (measured in N) and depends on gravitational field strength
exam.tip: Give one clear statement about each quantity, ideally with units.

exam.q: Name the piece of equipment used to measure weight.
model: Newton meter / calibrated spring balance / forcemeter
exam.tip: Balance or scales alone is not enough.

exam.q: A student hangs masses from a newton meter and records the weight for each. Describe how she should use the newton meter to obtain accurate readings.
model: Check the newton meter reads zero before adding masses / correct zero error
Hold the newton meter vertically and wait until the mass stops moving/bouncing
Read the scale at eye level (perpendicular) to avoid parallax
Choose a newton meter with a suitable range / resolution
exam.tip: Any three distinct practical points score; be specific about how, not just 'be careful'.

exam.q: The student plots a graph of weight against mass. The graph is a straight line through the origin. State the relationship shown and what the gradient represents.
model: Weight is directly proportional to mass
The gradient is the gravitational field strength, g
exam.tip: 'Directly proportional' needs both straight line and origin; say directly.

exam.q: A probe of mass 350 kg has a weight of 1295 N on Mars. Calculate the gravitational field strength on Mars.
model: g = W / m
g = 3.7 N/kg
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting so the method mark is clear.

exam.q: Explain why a hammer and a feather dropped together on the Moon hit the ground at the same time, even though the hammer has a much larger weight.
model: There is no air on the Moon so no air resistance; weight is the only force
The hammer has a larger weight but also a larger mass
acceleration = force / mass = (m x g) / m = g
So both accelerate at the same rate (g = 1.6 m/s²) and land together
exam.tip: Link W = m x g to F = m x a; the mass cancels.

exam.q: A crate on Earth has a weight of 4.2 kN. Calculate its mass in kg.
model: m = 420 kg
exam.tip: Convert kN to N before dividing.

exam.q: Discuss why an object's weight would be different on another planet but its mass would not. In your answer refer to what affects gravitational field strength.
model: Mass is the amount of matter in the object
The number of particles does not change when the object is moved, so mass is constant
Weight is the gravitational force on the object, W = m x g
Gravitational field strength depends on the mass of the planet
and on the distance from the centre of the planet (its radius)
A different planet has a different g, so the same mass gives a different weight; weight is proportional to g
exam.tip: A 6-mark answer needs a logical chain: define both, give the equation, explain what changes g, conclude.

worked.q: A student has a mass of 52 kg. Calculate her weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) and on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg).
steps: Write the equation: W = m x g
Mass is still 52 kg in both places
worked.ans: 520 N on Earth; 83.2 N (about 83 N) on the Moon.

worked.q: A newton meter shows that a rock weighs 3.6 N on Earth. Calculate the rock's mass in grams.
On planet X a 15 kg mass has a weight of 165 N. A lander weighs 6600 N on planet X. Calculate the lander's weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg).
steps: g on planet X = W / m = 165 / 15 = 11 N/kg

phy_edx.1.8.summary: In this core practical a trolley is pulled along a runway by a string that runs over a pulley to a hanging mass, and light gates (or a ticker timer or stopwatch and markers) are used to find its acceleration. You vary either the accelerating force (the weight of the hanging masses) or the mass being accelerated, keeping the other constant, to show that acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force and inversely proportional to mass. The results confirm Newton's second law, F = m x a, and the analysis uses a = (v - u) / t or v² - u² = 2ax.

core.h: Aim and link to Newton's second law
core.p: The aim is to **investigate the relationship between force, mass and acceleration** by varying the masses added to a trolley or hanger. Newton's second law says **resultant force = mass x acceleration (F = m x a)**, so we expect acceleration to rise with force and fall with mass.
bullets: Prediction 1: for a fixed mass, **acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force** (a ∝ F).
Prediction 2: for a fixed force, **acceleration is inversely proportional to mass** (a ∝ 1/m).
The experiment has two parts: vary force (mass constant), then vary mass (force constant).
Only one independent variable is changed in each part, so it is a fair test.
This practical can be assessed in written exam questions on method, analysis and evaluation.

callouts.p: F = m x a: the acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force on it and inversely proportional to its mass.

core.p: The standard set-up uses a trolley on a smooth runway (or bench) with a pulley clamped at the end. A string tied to the trolley runs over the pulley to a mass hanger. Timing is done with light gates connected to a data logger.
bullets: Trolley (or air-track glider to reduce friction).
Runway or ramp, with blocks to tilt it slightly to compensate for friction.
Bench pulley clamped to the end of the bench.
Light, inextensible string.
Mass hanger and slotted masses (for example 10 g or 100 g masses).
Two light gates and a data logger, plus a card (interrupt card) of known length mounted on the trolley.
Metre rule to measure the distance between the light gates.
Top-pan balance to measure the mass of the trolley and masses.
Alternative timing: ticker timer and tape, or stopwatch with marked distances (less accurate).

core.p: Identify the variables clearly; exam questions often ask for one independent, one dependent and two control variables.
bullets: **Part A independent variable**: the accelerating force (weight of hanging masses, W = m x g).
**Part B independent variable**: the mass of the trolley (add masses to the trolley).
**Dependent variable**: acceleration of the trolley.
**Control variables**: in part A the total mass of the system; in part B the hanging mass (force).
Also control: the slope/angle of the runway, the same trolley and surface, the distance between light gates, the length of the card, the release point (released from rest each time).

core.p: To test a ∝ F you increase the hanging mass while keeping the **total mass being accelerated constant**. The trick is to start with slotted masses on the trolley and move them one at a time onto the hanger.
bullets: Set up the runway, pulley, trolley and string; position two light gates a measured distance apart along the runway.
Tilt the runway slightly so the trolley just keeps moving at a steady speed when nudged with nothing on the hanger (friction compensated).
Place several masses on the trolley and one on the hanger.
Release the trolley from rest at the same start line each time.
Record the velocity at each light gate (data logger calculates v = card length / time to pass) and the time between gates.
Calculate acceleration.
Move one mass from the trolley to the hanger, so the force increases but the total mass stays the same; repeat.
Repeat each force at least three times and calculate a mean acceleration.
Stop the trolley safely at the end of the runway (use a buffer or catch it).

callouts.t: Why move masses from trolley to hanger?
callouts.p: The hanging mass is also being accelerated. Transferring masses keeps the total accelerated mass (trolley + hanger) constant, so force is the only thing changing.

core.p: To test a ∝ 1/m, keep the hanging mass constant (so the accelerating force is constant) and add masses to the trolley.
bullets: Keep the same hanging mass throughout, for example 100 g giving a force of 0.1 x 10 = 1 N.
Measure the mass of the trolley with a top-pan balance.
Add a known mass to the trolley each time (for example 200 g steps).
Release from rest at the same point and measure the acceleration as before.
Repeat each mass three times and calculate a mean.
Record total mass = trolley + added masses (+ hanging mass if analysing the whole system).

core.p: Light gates measure how long the card takes to pass through the beam. Speed = card length / time. With two light gates you get two speeds, from which acceleration can be found in two ways.
bullets: Speed at a gate: v = length of card / time card blocks the beam.
Method 1: **a = (v - u) / t**, where t is the time taken to travel between the gates.
Method 2: **v² - u² = 2 x a x x**, rearranged to a = (v² - u²) / (2x), where x is the distance between the gates.
A single light gate with a double interrupt card (two segments) can also give two speeds and the time between them.
Units: lengths in m, times in s, so a is in m/s².
Convert card lengths in cm to m before calculating.

callouts.p: If you are given the distance between gates, use v² - u² = 2ax. If you are given the time between gates, use a = (v - u) / t.

core.p: The accelerating force comes from the **weight of the hanging masses**, found using W = m x g with g = 10 N/kg.
bullets: Example: 50 g on the hanger: W = 0.05 x 10 = 0.5 N.
Include the mass of the hanger itself (often 10 g or 100 g).
If friction is compensated, the resultant force on the whole system is approximately this weight.
Strictly, the tension in the string is a little less than the hanging weight because the hanging mass is also accelerating; using total mass in F = m x a avoids this error.

callouts.p: Plot force in newtons, not hanging mass in grams, unless the question says otherwise.

core.p: Plot graphs to reveal the relationships. A straight line through the origin shows direct proportionality.
bullets: **Acceleration against force** (mass constant): straight line through the origin, so a ∝ F.
The gradient of the a-F graph = 1 / m (the reciprocal of the total mass).
**Acceleration against mass** (force constant): a curve, acceleration decreases as mass increases.
**Acceleration against 1/mass**: straight line through the origin, so a ∝ 1/m; gradient = F.
If the a-F line does not pass through the origin, friction has not been fully compensated (intercept on the force axis) or the runway is tilted too much (intercept on the acceleration axis).

core.p: Grade 9 answers explain **why** each step improves the results, not just what to do.
bullets: **Light gates instead of a stopwatch**: removes human reaction time error, which is large compared with the short times measured.
**Compensate for friction** by tilting the runway, so the resultant force is just the weight of the hanging masses.
**Repeat and average** to reduce the effect of random errors; discard anomalous results before averaging.
Use a long runway / gates far apart so times and velocity changes are larger and percentage uncertainty is smaller.
Make sure the string is parallel to the runway so the whole tension acts along the direction of motion.
Check the card passes fully and squarely through each beam.
Release from rest without pushing; a push gives an extra unmeasured force.
Use an air track to reduce friction further.

callouts.p: Repeats reduce random error. Friction and a zero error on a balance are systematic errors; repeats do not remove them.

core.p: The risks are low, but exams sometimes ask for one hazard and how to reduce it.
bullets: Falling masses could injure feet: place a box or soft cushion under the hanging masses.
Trolley could run off the end of the bench: use a buffer or catch it, and clamp the pulley firmly.
Keep the runway clear and do not stand in line with the moving trolley.
Do not use very large masses that make the trolley move too fast to stop.

core.p: You may be given a table of results to process. Calculate means, identify anomalies and use the graph to draw a conclusion linked to F = m x a.
bullets: Mean = sum of repeats / number of repeats (ignore anomalous values).
Range of repeats shows the spread; a larger range means less precise data.
Uncertainty is about half the range.
Draw a line of best fit, not dot-to-dot.
Conclusion language: 'As the force increases, the acceleration increases. The graph is a straight line through the origin, so acceleration is directly proportional to force.'
Use the gradient to calculate the mass being accelerated: m = 1 / gradient.

analogy.p: Pushing an empty supermarket trolley harder makes it speed up faster (more force, more acceleration). Pushing equally hard on a trolley full of bottles makes it speed up more slowly (more mass, less acceleration). In the lab the 'push' is the weight of the hanging masses and the light gates do the job of judging how fast it speeds up. Where it breaks down: your push is not steady and changes as you walk, and friction from the wheels is large; in the experiment the force is a constant weight and we compensate for friction by tilting the runway.

terms.d: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
The rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s²; a = (v - u) / t.
The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force on it and inversely proportional to its mass; F = m x a.
A sensor with a beam of light that records when and for how long an object blocks the beam, connected to a data logger.
A card of known length attached to the trolley that breaks the light gate beam; speed = card length / time blocked.
A device that records and processes measurements from sensors automatically.
In this practical, the weight of the hanging masses, W = m x g.
Tilting the runway so that a component of the trolley's weight balances friction, leaving the hanging weight as the resultant force.
The variable that you deliberately change.
The variable that you measure, which changes in response.
A variable kept the same so that the test is fair.
When one quantity doubles the other doubles; graph is a straight line through the origin.
When one quantity doubles the other halves; a graph against the reciprocal is a straight line through the origin.
Unpredictable variation in readings that is reduced by repeating and averaging.
An error that shifts every reading by the same amount or in the same direction, such as uncompensated friction.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others and should be repeated or left out of the mean.

mistakes.w: Independent variable: the trolley.
mistakes.r: The independent variable is the accelerating force (weight of hanging masses) or the mass of the trolley; name a quantity.

mistakes.w: Use a stopwatch because it is more accurate.
mistakes.r: Use light gates because they remove human reaction time error.

mistakes.w: Repeat the experiment to make it more accurate (no reason).
mistakes.r: Repeat and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of random errors and identify anomalies.

mistakes.w: Add masses to the hanger from the bench to increase the force.
mistakes.r: Move masses from the trolley to the hanger so the total mass accelerated stays constant.

mistakes.w: Acceleration is proportional to mass.
mistakes.r: Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (for a constant force).

mistakes.w: The force is the mass on the hanger, 50 g.
mistakes.r: The force is the weight: 0.05 kg x 10 N/kg = 0.5 N.

mistakes.w: As force increases acceleration increases, so they are proportional.
mistakes.r: They are directly proportional only if the graph is a straight line through the origin.

mistakes.w: a = v / t using the final speed only.
mistakes.r: a = (v - u) / t using the change in velocity between the two gates, or a = (v² - u²) / 2x.

exam.q: State the dependent variable when investigating how force affects acceleration.
model: Acceleration (of the trolley)
exam.tip: One word answers are fine if they name the correct quantity.

exam.q: Give two control variables when investigating the effect of mass on acceleration.
model: Accelerating force / hanging mass
Any one other: angle of runway, distance between light gates, same surface/trolley, length of card
exam.tip: Two different variables; 'same equipment' is too vague.

exam.q: Explain why light gates give more accurate results than a stopwatch.
model: Stopwatch timing involves human reaction time
which is large compared with the short times being measured / light gates record times automatically to a higher resolution
exam.tip: Give the reason (reaction time) and why it matters.

exam.q: A 0.05 kg mass hangs from the string. Calculate the accelerating force. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: F = W = m x g = 0.05 x 10
exam.tip: Convert grams to kg first.

exam.q: The card on the trolley is 0.10 m long and blocks the first light gate for 0.25 s and the second for 0.10 s. The trolley takes 0.60 s between the gates. Calculate the acceleration.
model: a = 1.0 m/s²
exam.tip: Find both speeds first, then the change in velocity.

exam.q: Explain why the runway is tilted slightly before the experiment.
model: To compensate for (balance) friction
so that the resultant force is (equal to) the weight of the hanging masses / trolley moves at constant speed with no hanging mass
exam.tip: Say what it cancels and what that leaves as the resultant force.

exam.q: Explain why the student moves masses from the trolley to the hanger, rather than adding new masses to the hanger.
model: The hanging masses are also accelerated / are part of the mass of the system
so moving them keeps the total mass constant, making force the only variable changed
exam.tip: Mention fair test: one independent variable.

exam.q: A graph of acceleration against force is a straight line through the origin with gradient 2.0 kg^-1 (m/s² per N). Calculate the mass of the system.
model: gradient = a / F = 1 / m
exam.tip: From F = m a, a = (1/m) F, so gradient = 1/m.

exam.q: A student's graph of acceleration against force does not pass through the origin; it cuts the force axis at 0.2 N. Suggest a reason.
model: Friction has not been fully compensated
so 0.2 N of force is needed just to overcome friction before the trolley accelerates
exam.tip: Link the intercept to a specific systematic error.

exam.q: Describe how a student could investigate how the mass of a trolley affects its acceleration. Include how to make the results valid and reliable.
model: Trolley on runway, string over pulley to hanging mass; two light gates with card on trolley
Tilt runway to compensate for friction
Keep the hanging mass (force) constant
Measure trolley mass with a balance; add known masses to the trolley in steps
Release from rest from the same point; record speeds at gates and time/distance between them
Calculate acceleration using a = (v - u) / t or v² - u² = 2ax
Repeat each mass three times and take a mean, ignoring anomalies
Plot a against 1/m; straight line through origin shows a inversely proportional to m
exam.tip: Level 3 answers give a logical sequence: set-up, control, measurement, calculation, repeats, analysis.

exam.q: Predict what happens to the acceleration if the force is kept constant and the total mass is doubled.
model: Acceleration halves
exam.tip: Inversely proportional: double one, halve the other.

worked.q: Two light gates are 0.50 m apart. A trolley passes the first at 0.30 m/s and the second at 0.80 m/s. Calculate its acceleration.
steps: Use v² - u² = 2 x a x x

worked.q: In part A the total mass is 0.80 kg. A hanging mass of 120 g is used (friction compensated). Predict the acceleration and compare with a measured value of 1.4 m/s².
steps: Likely reason: friction not fully compensated or air resistance, so resultant force is a little less than 1.2 N
worked.ans: Predicted 1.5 m/s²; measured value is slightly lower because of remaining friction.

worked.q: Results (force constant at 1.0 N): mass 0.5 kg, a = 2.0 m/s²; 1.0 kg, a = 1.0 m/s²; 2.0 kg, a = 0.5 m/s². What do these show?
steps: Each time mass doubles, acceleration halves
m x a = 1.0 in every case, equal to the force
So a = F / m: acceleration is inversely proportional to mass
A graph of a against 1/m would be a straight line through the origin with gradient 1.0 N
worked.ans: Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass, confirming F = m x a.

phy_edx.1.9.summary: An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity, because velocity is a vector and its direction is changing all the time. A changing velocity means the object is accelerating, and by Newton's laws an acceleration needs a resultant force. For circular motion this resultant force, called the centripetal force, always acts towards the centre of the circle and is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity.

core.h: Speed versus velocity in circular motion
core.p: **Speed** is a scalar (size only) but **velocity** is a vector: speed in a given direction. An object going round a circle at a steady speed is always changing direction, so even though its speed is constant **its velocity is changing**.
bullets: At every point the velocity is along the **tangent** to the circle, in the direction of motion.
The size of the velocity (the speed) stays the same; only its direction changes.
Two velocities are only equal if they have the same speed **and** the same direction.
So 'constant speed' and 'constant velocity' mean different things for circular motion.
This is a qualitative idea at GCSE: you explain it in words and diagrams, not with an equation.

callouts.p: An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because its direction is continuously changing.

core.p: **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity. Because the velocity of an object in circular motion is changing (in direction), the object **is accelerating** even though it is not speeding up or slowing down.
bullets: Acceleration is a vector, so a change of direction counts as acceleration.
For uniform circular motion the acceleration is directed **towards the centre of the circle**.
This surprises people because in everyday language 'accelerate' means 'go faster'.
In physics, speeding up, slowing down and changing direction are all accelerations.

callouts.p: The rate of change of velocity. A change in speed, direction or both is an acceleration.

core.p: Newton's first law says that an object keeps moving at a constant velocity (in a straight line at steady speed) unless a **resultant force** acts on it. Circular motion is not a straight line, so there **must be a resultant force**. Newton's second law (F = m x a) tells us the force is in the same direction as the acceleration: towards the centre.
bullets: No resultant force means a straight-line path at constant speed.
A resultant force at right angles to the motion changes direction but not speed.
A resultant force along the motion changes speed instead.
The force and acceleration are always in the same direction.

core.p: The resultant force that keeps an object moving in a circle is called the **centripetal force**. 'Centripetal' means 'centre-seeking': the force always acts **towards the centre of the circle**.
bullets: Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the name for the **resultant** force towards the centre.
It is always provided by a real force: tension, friction, gravity, the normal contact force, or electrostatic attraction.
On a diagram draw it as an arrow from the object towards the centre.
It is **perpendicular (at 90°) to the velocity** at every instant.
As the object moves the direction of the force changes too, so it keeps pointing at the centre.

callouts.p: The resultant force acting on an object moving in a circle, directed towards the centre of the circle.

core.p: The centripetal force acts at right angles to the direction the object is moving. A force at right angles has no part acting forwards or backwards along the motion, so it cannot speed the object up or slow it down; it only **turns** it.
bullets: Force perpendicular to velocity: changes direction only.
No component of force along the motion, so no change of speed.
Because the object does not move towards or away from the centre, the force does no work and the kinetic energy stays constant.
If the force were not exactly towards the centre, the speed would also change.

callouts.p: Centripetal force changes the direction of the velocity, not its size.

core.h: What happens if the centripetal force is removed
core.p: If the centripetal force suddenly disappears, there is no longer a resultant force, so the object carries on in a **straight line along the tangent** at the point where the force stopped (Newton's first law). It does **not** fly outwards along the radius.
bullets: String snaps on a whirled ball: the ball flies off along the tangent.
Car on an icy bend: not enough friction, so the car slides straight on, off the outside of the bend.
Mud flying off a spinning bicycle wheel leaves along the tangent.
In a spin dryer, water is not pushed outwards; the holes stop providing a force on the water so it carries straight on through them while the clothes are held in.

callouts.p: Do not say the object is thrown outwards by a 'centrifugal force'. It moves off along the tangent because there is no resultant force.

core.h: Examples: what provides the centripetal force
core.p: In every case, identify the real force pointing towards the centre of the circle.
bullets: Ball on a string whirled in a horizontal circle: **tension** in the string.
Car going round a roundabout or bend: **friction** between the tyres and the road.
Moon orbiting the Earth, Earth orbiting the Sun, artificial satellites: **gravitational force (gravity)**.
Electron orbiting a nucleus (simple model): **electrostatic attraction**.
Clothes in a spinning washing machine drum: **normal contact force** from the drum wall.
Cyclist leaning into a bend: friction from the road on the tyres.

core.p: Planets, moons and satellites move in (nearly) circular orbits at (nearly) constant speed. **Gravity** provides the centripetal force, always pulling towards the centre of the larger body.
bullets: A satellite in a circular orbit has constant speed but changing velocity.
It is continuously accelerating towards the Earth (it is in free fall), but its sideways motion means it keeps missing the ground.
Without gravity it would travel off in a straight line along the tangent.
The force of gravity is perpendicular to the satellite's velocity in a circular orbit, so its speed is constant.

callouts.p: Use the same three steps: direction changes, so velocity changes, so it accelerates; gravity is the resultant force towards the centre.

core.h: Factors affecting the size of the force needed
core.p: You do not need an equation for centripetal force at GCSE, but you should understand qualitatively what makes a bigger centripetal force necessary. More force is needed when the object has to change direction more sharply or has more mass.
bullets: **Greater mass**: more force needed for the same circle and speed (F = m x a).
**Greater speed**: more force needed; a faster car on the same bend needs much more friction.
**Smaller radius** (tighter circle): more force needed.
If the available force (for example friction) is less than the force needed, the object cannot follow the circle and moves outward of the curve, towards a straight tangent path.
This is why roads have lower speed limits on sharp bends and why wet or icy roads are dangerous on corners.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to add arrows to a diagram of an object in a circle. Be precise about which arrow is which.
bullets: **Velocity arrow**: tangent to the circle, in the direction of travel.
**Centripetal force arrow**: from the object towards the centre, at 90° to the velocity.
**Acceleration arrow**: same direction as the centripetal force (towards the centre).
Path if force removed: straight line along the tangent.
Use a ruler; arrows at 90° to each other must look perpendicular.

callouts.p: Velocity along the tangent, force along the radius: they should form an L shape at the object.

core.h: Linking explanation chain for 4 and 6 mark answers
core.p: Top answers link each idea to the next with 'so' or 'because'. Learn this chain and adapt it to any example.
bullets: The object's direction is constantly changing.
Velocity is a vector, so the velocity is changing even though the speed is constant.
A changing velocity is an acceleration.
By Newton's first/second law an acceleration requires a resultant force.
This resultant force is the centripetal force, acting towards the centre of the circle.
It is provided by (name the real force: tension, friction, gravity).
It acts perpendicular to the velocity, so the speed does not change.

analogy.t: Dog on a lead running round you
analogy.p: Imagine running a dog round you in a circle on a lead. The dog always wants to run straight ahead (its velocity is along the tangent), but the lead keeps pulling it towards you in the middle, so it keeps turning. The pull of the lead is the centripetal force: it always points at you, the centre. Let go and the dog runs off in a straight line, not directly away from you. Where it breaks down: a real dog can choose to change its speed or direction by using its legs, but an object in uniform circular motion has only the centre-pointing resultant force, which changes its direction without changing its speed.

terms.d: Motion of an object along a circular path.
A scalar quantity: distance travelled per unit time, with no direction.
A vector quantity: speed in a given direction.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction.
A quantity with magnitude only.
The rate of change of velocity; includes a change of direction.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
The resultant force on an object moving in a circle, acting towards the centre of the circle.
A straight line that touches the circle at one point, at right angles to the radius there; the direction of the velocity.
The distance from the centre of the circle to the path; the centripetal force acts along it.
At right angles (90°) to; centripetal force is perpendicular to velocity.
The curved path of a planet, moon or satellite around a larger body, maintained by gravity.
The pulling force in a stretched string, rope or cable.
A force that opposes the sliding of two surfaces; provides the centripetal force for a car on a bend.
An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.

mistakes.w: The ball is moving at constant speed so it is not accelerating.
mistakes.r: Its direction is changing, so its velocity is changing; it is accelerating towards the centre.

mistakes.w: The centripetal force acts outwards.
mistakes.r: The centripetal force acts towards the centre of the circle.

mistakes.w: When the string breaks the ball flies straight outwards.
mistakes.r: It moves off in a straight line along the tangent to the circle.

mistakes.w: Centripetal force is an extra force acting along with tension.
mistakes.r: The centripetal force is provided by the tension; it is the resultant force, not an additional force.

mistakes.w: The velocity is constant because the speed is constant.
mistakes.r: Velocity is a vector; the direction changes, so the velocity changes.

mistakes.w: Draws the velocity arrow pointing to the centre.
mistakes.r: Velocity is along the tangent; only the force and acceleration point to the centre.

mistakes.w: A satellite stays up because there is no gravity in space.
mistakes.r: Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps the satellite in orbit.

mistakes.w: The force makes the object speed up.
mistakes.r: The force is perpendicular to the motion so it changes direction only, not speed.

exam.q: State the direction of the resultant force on an object moving in a circle at constant speed.
model: Towards the centre of the circle
exam.tip: Say 'towards the centre'; 'inwards' alone may not be enough.

exam.q: Name the force that provides the centripetal force for the Moon orbiting the Earth.
model: Gravitational force / gravity (of the Earth on the Moon)
exam.tip: Weight is accepted on some mark schemes, but gravitational force is safest.

exam.q: Explain why a satellite moving in a circular orbit at constant speed is accelerating.
model: Its direction is (continuously) changing, so its velocity is changing
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity
exam.tip: Mention velocity explicitly; speed is constant, velocity is not.

exam.q: Name the force providing the centripetal force for a car driving round a roundabout.
model: Friction (between the tyres and the road)
exam.tip: Engine force and air resistance act along the motion, not towards the centre.

exam.q: A ball is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string. Draw and label arrows to show the velocity of the ball and the force on the ball from the string.
model: Velocity arrow along the tangent in the direction of motion
Force (tension) arrow along the string towards the centre
exam.tip: Use a ruler; the arrows should be at 90° to each other.

exam.q: The string in the previous question breaks. Describe the motion of the ball immediately afterwards (ignore gravity).
model: It moves in a straight line
along the tangent to the circle / in the direction of its velocity when the string broke, at constant speed
exam.tip: Not 'outwards' and not 'towards the centre'.

exam.q: Explain why the speed of an object in uniform circular motion stays constant even though a resultant force acts on it.
model: The resultant (centripetal) force acts perpendicular to the direction of motion
so it has no component along the motion and only changes the direction, not the speed
exam.tip: Key word: perpendicular / at right angles.

exam.q: Explain why a car is more likely to skid on a sharp bend when the road is icy.
model: A centripetal force towards the centre of the bend is needed to change the car's direction
This is provided by friction between the tyres and the road
Ice reduces friction, so the force available is less than needed and the car continues in a straighter path / skids off the bend
exam.tip: Link the real force (friction) to the centripetal force requirement.

exam.q: Suggest two changes that would increase the centripetal force needed for a car to go round a bend.
model: Increasing the speed of the car
Decreasing the radius of the bend / increasing the mass of the car
exam.tip: Any two from speed, mass, radius, with the correct direction of change.

exam.q: A child swings a conker on a string in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Explain, in terms of forces and velocity, why the conker moves in a circle.
model: The direction of the conker is continuously changing so its velocity changes
so the conker is accelerating
an acceleration requires a resultant force (Newton's first/second law)
this is the tension in the string acting towards the centre of the circle (centripetal force)
exam.tip: Build a chain: direction, velocity, acceleration, resultant force, named force, direction.

exam.q: Explain how the Earth can travel around the Sun at a constant speed while its velocity changes. In your answer refer to the forces acting and to what would happen if the force stopped acting.
model: Velocity is a vector: speed in a given direction
The Earth's direction of motion is continuously changing as it orbits, so its velocity is changing
A changing velocity means the Earth is accelerating (towards the Sun)
An acceleration needs a resultant force: the gravitational attraction of the Sun
This centripetal force acts towards the centre of the orbit, perpendicular to the Earth's velocity, so it changes direction but not speed
If gravity stopped, there would be no resultant force and the Earth would move off in a straight line along the tangent at constant speed
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need the full linked argument plus the 'force removed' consequence.

worked.q: Model answer: a hammer thrower spins a hammer in a circle and then releases it. Explain the path of the hammer before and after release.
steps: Before release: the hammer moves in a circle; its direction changes continuously, so its velocity changes and it accelerates towards the centre.
The resultant force causing this is the tension in the wire, acting towards the centre (centripetal force).
At release the tension becomes zero, so (ignoring air resistance and gravity) there is no resultant force horizontally.
By Newton's first law it continues at constant velocity, in a straight line along the tangent at the release point.
worked.ans: Circular path held by tension towards the centre; after release it travels along the tangent, not outwards along the radius.

worked.q: Applied example: identify the centripetal force and the effect of increasing speed for (a) a satellite orbit, (b) a cyclist on a bend.
steps: (a) Satellite: gravitational force of the Earth, towards the Earth's centre.
A higher speed at the same height would need a larger centripetal force than gravity provides, so the satellite would move to a wider path.
(b) Cyclist: friction between tyres and road, towards the centre of the bend.
Higher speed needs more friction; if the needed force exceeds the maximum friction, the bike skids outward from the curve.
worked.ans: (a) gravity, (b) friction; in both, more speed needs a larger centripetal force.

worked.q: A car travels once around a circular track at a constant speed of 20 m/s. Compare its speed and velocity at the start and at the halfway point.
steps: Speed at both points is 20 m/s, as the speed is constant.
At the halfway point the car is travelling in the opposite direction to the start.
So the velocity has changed from 20 m/s in one direction to 20 m/s in the opposite direction.
The velocity has changed, so the car accelerated, caused by friction acting towards the centre.
worked.ans: Same speed (20 m/s) but different velocity: equal size, opposite direction.
